**No rhetorical question as the first line of any asset.** Blog post, landing page hero, email (subject line and first sentence both), LinkedIn post, X post, video script, slide one of a deck.

"Is your cluster ready for the next incident?" tells the reader nothing and asks them to do the writer's work. It's also the most common opening in our category, so it reads as noise. Open on a fact, an event or a claim.

| Don't open with | Open with |
|---|---|
| What would you do if a pod started a shell at 3am? | A pod in `checkout` started a shell at 03:14 UTC. |
| Tired of alert fatigue? | Most alerts at 3am are about something that already stopped mattering. |

Real questions later in a piece are fine. An FAQ section is full of them and that's what it is for, as long as the page opens on a statement.

"}, {"ref": "source_105", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "4. Positioning", "Testing a campaign idea"], "start_line": 162, "end_line": 172, "content": "### Testing a campaign idea

Before a concept goes to design, Ilse's team asks four questions of it.

1. Could any other security vendor run this with their logo on it? If so, it isn't the position.
2. Does it depend on the reader being scared? If so, drop it.
3. Does it show containment, or only talk about it?
4. Would the customer's on-call lead forward it to a colleague without a sarcastic comment?

The "Quiet night" concept from the 2026 launch passed all four, and it became the opening of the launch film: a dark office, one screen, a log line reading that a pod had been isolated, and an engineer who doesn't appear because she is asleep at home.

"}, {"ref": "source_106", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "4. Positioning", "Where the category goes wrong"], "start_line": 150, "end_line": 161, "content": "### Where the category goes wrong

Security marketing has habits that readers have learned to skip. The position is partly defined by not having them.

| Category habit | What Wickhold does |
|---|---|
| Opens with a frightening scenario | Opens with what a team can do about the problem |
| Promises total coverage | Says what is covered and names what is not |
| Sells the dashboard | Shows the containment action and its log entry |
| Treats the on-call engineer as a victim | Treats the on-call engineer as the expert |
| Uses a survey to alarm | Uses a survey to size a problem, then stops |

"}, {"ref": "source_107", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "7. Color", "What replaced Cobalt"], "start_line": 298, "end_line": 303, "content": "### What replaced Cobalt

Cobalt, the primary color from 2024, was retired on February 10, 2026, and **Ember `#C2501F` replaced it as the primary color**. Cobalt should not appear in any new work. Ember is not used the way Cobalt was. Cobalt covered whole slides, hero bands and booth walls. Ember is a small, deliberate point of heat, and a layout built around it should look mostly like Tallow or Soot.

The reasons for the change were practical as well as symbolic. The category is full of blue, and in side-by-side tests of competitor pages Wickhold's old pages were hard to pick out. A warm orange-brown also ties the color to the brand idea, since it is the color of a banked coal. It is deliberately neither a bright hazard orange nor an alarm red, because the brand is not trying to raise a reader's pulse.

1. Decide the category and read that page.
2. Decide the content type and read that page.
3. Search the library. Search by description and by a few different words, since tags are uneven.

"}, {"ref": "source_111", "relative_path": "brand/voice/voice-and-tone-2026.md", "heading_path": ["Wickhold voice and tone", "Tone by channel"], "start_line": 123, "end_line": 136, "content": "**The Containment Report.** Annual, every April, and the most formal thing we publish. It reads like a clinical note: findings in flat declaratives, method stated early, no pitch in the body. The product can appear at the end, briefly, once the reader has had what they came for.

**Release notes.** Past tense, specific, no selling. A bug we fixed is described as a bug.

**Press.** Third person, plain, one idea per release. The quote from Maren is the only place with any warmth, and she writes it herself.

**Sales decks and talk tracks.** Same facts, same claims, slightly warmer because a person is in the room. If a slide would embarrass the on-call lead, it comes out.

**Webinars and video.** Script it as speech, then cut a third. Two people talking through a real incident timeline beats one person reading slides. No stock intro music with a heartbeat in it, and no voiceover that sounds like a trailer.

**Support replies.** These are written by the support team and we don't police them, but the same habit applies: repeat what you saw, say what you did, say what happens next. A reply that begins by thanking the customer for their patience has already lost them.

**Events.** Slow Burn Summit in Denver is the one place where we are among friends, and it can sound like that. The stage voice is relaxed and first-name, and the facts on the slides are still the facts. Field Day is smaller and closer to a conversation in a car park. Booth copy is brand voice: short, mechanical, no shouting.

"}, {"ref": "source_117", "relative_path": "brand/style/capitalization-product-names.md", "heading_path": ["Capitalization + product names (quick sheet)"], "start_line": 1, "end_line": 39, "content": "# Capitalization + product names (quick sheet)

Pinned for the web team after three separate spellings turned up on one page.

Full form on first mention, short form after. First mention means the first place the name appears in a piece, and a headline counts.

| First mention | After that |
|---|---|
| Wickhold Quenchline | Quenchline |
| Wickhold Evenburn | Evenburn |
| Wickhold Leashgate | Leashgate |

One capital each. Never QuenchLine, EvenBurn or LeashGate. No internal caps, no hyphens, no all-caps in slides or nav.

Each piece starts over. A blog post that says Wickhold Quenchline does not earn the short form in the email promoting it.

Evenburn took its name on March 2, 2026. Don't write the former name in current copy, including "formerly" lines. Support handles customers who still ask for it.

Right: "Wickhold Evenburn ranks drift by exposure path. Evenburn does not contain anything at runtime."

Wrong: "Evenburn ranks drift" as the opening line, with the full name saved for the footer.

Nav labels and pricing table rows can use the short form. The page's first heading or sentence still uses the full one.

Never combine products into one name ("Quenchline-Evenburn suite"). There is no suite. If you mean more than one, name them.

**Company:** Wickhold. "Wickhold Security" retired with the rebrand on February 10, 2026. Wickhold, Inc. appears in contracts and legal footers and nowhere else.

**Lowercase, always:** contain mode, observe mode, containment action, default containment policy, drift, exposure path, fix order, tool-call policy, agent identity. These are concepts, not features with a logo.

**Capitalized:** tiers (Core, Team, Enterprise), Slow Burn Summit, Field Day, Wickhold Containment Report. "The report" on second reference, lowercase. Series A and Series B take capitals; SOC 2 Type II is set as shown.

Possessives are fine (Quenchline's agent). Skip the article: "Quenchline contains", never "the Quenchline".

The report had a different name before 2025: Wickhold Field Report. Keep that name when citing an edition that carried it. Don't rename old editions.

Feature names don't get "Wickhold" in front of them, and they don't get a trademark symbol. Neither do the products in running copy.

Lowercase product names only in code, where the tool demands it.
"}, {"ref": "source_118", "relative_path": "brand/voice/voice-and-tone-2026.md", "heading_path": ["Wickhold voice and tone", "One rewrite, start to finish"], "start_line": 235, "end_line": 256, "content": "## One rewrite, start to finish

A draft that came through in May, lightly disguised:

> We're excited to announce that we think our powerful new drift capabilities will transform how modern teams approach cloud risk, giving you the confidence you need in an increasingly dangerous world.

The edit went like this.

"We're excited to announce" went first. The reader's interest in our excitement is zero.

"We think" is out, because this is brand voice.

"Powerful", "new" and "modern" were doing nothing. Remove them and the sentence gets more honest and no less informative.

"Increasingly dangerous world" is the fear habit, and it also isn't something we can source.

That left "drift capabilities will transform how teams approach cloud risk", which on inspection means nothing. So the reviewer asked the only useful question: what does a person see on the screen? The product manager's answer became the copy.

> Wickhold Evenburn lists the drift in a cluster and ranks it by exposure path, so the fix order is on one page. It does not contain anything at runtime.

That is shorter, it can be checked, and it names an edge. Nobody involved felt that it was a loss.

"}, {"ref": "source_120", "relative_path": "brand/legal/regional-rules-eu-uk.md", "heading_path": ["Regional rules: EU and UK copy", "GDPR wording"], "start_line": 7, "end_line": 34, "content": "### GDPR wording

Never say "GDPR compliant". Not about Wickhold, its products, its customers' deployments or any feature. The ban began with EU and UK copy and it now applies everywhere, including US pages that a European buyer can obviously read.

The approved wording is:

> Wickhold supports customers' GDPR obligations.

Use it as written. GDPR obligations belong to the controller and the processor and depend on what they do with the data. No vendor product can make a customer compliant, and a regulator or a procurement lawyer will read the phrase as a promise.

Variants that have turned up in drafts, all refused:

- "GDPR-ready"
- "fully GDPR aligned"
- "compliant with EU privacy law"
- "UK GDPR certified"

If a UK reader needs the point spelled out, the approved sentence covers UK GDPR. Do not add a second claim.

Examples:

| Bad | Good |
|---|---|
| Our GDPR compliant platform keeps EU workloads safe. | Wickhold supports customers' GDPR obligations. |
| Quenchline makes your clusters GDPR compliant. | Wickhold Quenchline records each containment action with a timestamp. Wickhold supports customers' GDPR obligations. |

A word on tone. European security buyers we've met through Field Day meetups tend to ask for the document and not the promise, so a short, flat statement does better than a paragraph about how seriously we take privacy. If a page has one line on GDPR, the approved sentence is that line. Don't surround it with "privacy-first" or "by design", which raise the same problem in softer words.

"}, {"ref": "source_121", "relative_path": "brand/archive/blog/comparison-quenchline-vs-tesserline-2026.md", "heading_path": ["Comparison: Wickhold Quenchline and Tesserline for runtime containment", "Overhead and deployment"], "start_line": 35, "end_line": 45, "content": "## Overhead and deployment

Both products run agents on the node. Quenchline's agent is eBPF-based and runs at under 2% CPU overhead on a typical node, in Wickhold lab benchmarks, 2026. We have not run a side-by-side benchmark against Tesserline, and we won't publish a number we did not measure. Test both on a representative node pool with your own workloads, because the mix of syscalls matters more than any vendor's headline figure.

During the trial, check these things with either product:

- Which kernel versions and node images are supported on your managed Kubernetes service
- How the agent behaves when it loses contact with its control plane
- What happens to alerting during an agent upgrade
- How exceptions are written, reviewed and expired

"}, {"ref": "source_122", "relative_path": "brand/archive/landing/quenchline-landing-current.md", "heading_path": ["Runtime containment for Kubernetes, decided before the incident", "What Quenchline does not do"], "start_line": 48, "end_line": 51, "content": "## What Quenchline does not do

Quenchline does not fix the cause. It holds a failure where it is, and it leaves the workload degraded on purpose until someone on your team repairs it. It also covers Kubernetes only, so workloads on plain virtual machines stay outside its view.

"}, {"ref": "source_123", "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md", "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "4. Numbers", "Everything else"], "start_line": 82, "end_line": 92, "content": "### Everything else

- **Measurements take digits, always.** Anything with a unit: 220 nodes, 11 minutes, 7.4 hours, 90 days, 38 seconds, 1,900 nodes.
- **Counts of ordinary things** spell out one to nine and use digits from 10: "three clusters", "12 namespaces". Mixed in one sentence, go with digits.
- **Commas from 1,000 up.** No "1.9k nodes", not even on social.
- **Keep the decimal the source gave you.** 7.4 hours stays 7.4 hours. Don't round to "about seven hours", and don't add precision the source lacks.
- **Approved sentences stay as approved.** The report line says "more than six hours", spelled out, and that's how it runs in every piece. The same goes for "more than 140 customers", which never becomes "140+". Legal approved the sentence, and this guide doesn't get to tidy it.
- **Don't do arithmetic on claims.** Lowmoor went from 4 hours to 11 minutes. Do not convert that into a percentage or an "x times faster". The figures we can stand behind are the two figures we were given. Same for adding results from different customers together.
- **No "up to".** "Up to" numbers are a best case wearing a fact's clothes. Give the median, or say which run you mean.
- **No tildes or "approx."** in published copy. If a figure is an estimate, say "about".

"}, {"ref": "source_128", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/00-visual-rules-common.md", "heading_path": ["Visual rules common to every image", "The image library and its metadata"], "start_line": 63, "end_line": 81, "content": "## The image library and its metadata

Every approved image lives in the image library, and every image in it has a metadata record. Do not pick from the thumbnail grid and stop there. The thumbnail does not show you the limits on the image.

| Field | What it tells you |
|---|---|
| `id`, `filename` | Identity. Filenames were set by different people across several years and tell you little. |
| `type`, `title` | Rough category and a human label. |
| `description` | What is in the picture. Often thin, sometimes empty. |
| `tags` | Search help. Inconsistent, so never treat a missing tag as meaning anything. |
| `usage_rights` | The grant we hold for the file. |
| `restrictions` | The limits on this particular image. See below. |
| `added_date` | When it entered the library, which is not when it was made. |
| `source`, `attribution` | Where it came from. In-house work reads `internal-production`, and `attribution` is usually empty or names the in-house team. Empty attribution means no credit line is needed. |
| `width`, `height` | Pixel size. Check before you plan a crop. |
| `background` | How the image relates to what sits behind it. See below. |
| `safe_on` | Which grounds it can sit on. See below. |
| `variant_of` | Points at the parent when the image is one version of another. |

"}, {"ref": "source_129", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "11. Governance"], "start_line": 451, "end_line": 454, "content": "## 11. Governance

"}, {"ref": "source_130", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "3. Values", "The values at work"], "start_line": 109, "end_line": 117, "content": "### The values at work

"}, {"ref": "source_131", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "9. Photography and illustration direction", "What fits and what doesn't"], "start_line": 407, "end_line": 415, "content": "### What fits and what doesn't

Bad: `Containment Report 2026 is out. Read the Containment Report 2026 today.`

"}, {"ref": "source_137", "relative_path": "brand/archive/landing/quenchline-landing-current.md", "heading_path": ["Runtime containment for Kubernetes, decided before the incident", "Containment actions"], "start_line": 34, "end_line": 41, "content": "## Containment actions

| Action | What happens | Use it when |
|---|---|---|
| Isolate a pod's network | The pod can no longer reach anything outside it | A workload is talking to something it never has |
| Freeze a process | Execution stops and memory stays intact | You want evidence for a human to read |
| Drain a node | Pods move off the node, within your PodDisruptionBudgets | The node itself is suspect |

"}, {"ref": "source_138", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "9. Photography and illustration direction", "Commissioning imagery"], "start_line": 416, "end_line": 423, "content": "### Commissioning imagery

A good image brief names the idea, where the image will run and its one focal point, and it leaves the style to the visual guidance. "A wick in a ring of cut paper, for a blog on containment policy" is a usable brief. "Something cool about AI security" is not.

Freelancers and agencies should get the visual guidance before their first sketch. On the launch film, the first round of location photos came back blue and spotless, because the agency had worked from a mood board built on the old identity. Reshooting took a week.

Any generated or composited image gets the same review as a commissioned one. It is held to the same direction, and a person looks at it at full size before it goes anywhere.

"}, {"ref": "source_139", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/00-visual-rules-common.md", "heading_path": ["Visual rules common to every image", "How the visual rules are layered"], "start_line": 7, "end_line": 20, "content": "## How the visual rules are layered

Three layers, read in this order.

1. **This page.** Applies to everything.
2. **The category.** What kind of image is it? Photo, illustration, icon, logo, product screenshot, chart, social graphic, event graphic, legal and trust imagery, anything showing a person.
3. **The content type.** Where is it going? Blog hero, LinkedIn, X, email header, landing page.

Most images touch one rule from each layer, and some touch two categories. A photo of a staff member at a customer site is photography and consent at once, and it has to pass both.

A lower layer can narrow a higher one. The illustration category accepts several formats, for example, and the blog hero page accepts fewer of them. In that case follow the narrower rule for that placement, and the broader rule stays true everywhere else. A lower layer cannot loosen this page. If a content-type page seems to let you do something this page forbids, bring it to Brand, because one of the two pages is wrong and we want to fix it.

Per-campaign exceptions go through Noor's exception log. Without an entry there, if a campaign needs something new, the rule changes for everybody or the campaign changes.

"}, {"ref": "source_142", "relative_path": "brand/channels/blog-playbook.md", "heading_path": ["Writing for the Wickhold blog", "5. Code and commands"], "start_line": 69, "end_line": 84, "content": "## 5. Code and commands

- Every code block must run. An engineer other than the author pastes it into a test cluster before publishing. Kofi keeps a throwaway cluster for this and will give you access.
- State versions at the top of the block or in the sentence before it: Kubernetes, Helm chart, kernel where it matters.
- Show the output when the output is the point, and trim it with a visible `...`.
- Use real-looking names like `payments-api` and `checkout`. Avoid `foo` and `my-app`, and don't use a customer's actual namespace names, even with permission.
- Say what fails. If `helm upgrade` can leave the agent in `CrashLoopBackOff` on an old kernel, put that in the post.

```bash
# Good: what you ran, and what to look for
kubectl get pods -n payments-api -o wide
# ...
# payments-api-6f9c7d   0/1   Terminating   0   3m   10.2.4.17   node-a
# A pod stuck here after a drain usually has a finalizer. Check that first.
```

"}, {"ref": "source_143", "relative_path": "brand/voice/word-list.md", "heading_path": ["Word list"], "start_line": 1, "end_line": 4, "content": "# Word list

Everything here applies to anything a customer, prospect, journalist or candidate can read. Slack can say what it likes.

"}, {"ref": "source_144", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/00-visual-rules-common.md", "heading_path": ["Visual rules common to every image", "Other rules for all images"], "start_line": 49, "end_line": 62, "content": "## Other rules for all images

**Current identity only.** Ember `#C2501F`, Soot `#15181C`, Tallow `#F4EFE6`, with Whetstone `#5E6B73` and Verdigris `#2F8F83` as secondary colors. Bricolage Grotesque, IBM Plex Sans and IBM Plex Mono for any type on an image. Anything leaning on the 2024 blue palette or the 2024 logo is out, however good it looks. Some of those images are still in the library with no flag on them, so your eye is part of this check.

**No third-party marks.** No real product logos on laptop lids, no cloud provider marks on diagrams, no conference logos in a crop unless the agreement with that organizer allows it. Customer marks are a legal matter and go through Legal first.

**No watermarks,** no preview overlays, no leftover crop marks. If an image arrived with a watermark, its rights are not what you think they are.

**Do not stretch, tint or recolor library files.** Crop freely within the category's limits. Stretching breaks the proportions of the art and recoloring breaks the palette. Filters are out too: the warm look comes from the source image, and a filter laid on a cool image only makes it look cool and filtered. If an image needs a color change to fit, it is the wrong image.

**Export for the placement.** WebP or PNG for web, PNG where transparency matters, SVG for logos and icons when the placement accepts it. Keep web images under 400 KB unless the content-type page says otherwise. JPEG artifacts around Ember shapes are very visible, so check flat illustration at full size after compressing.

**Nothing that frightens.** Images follow the same stance as the copy. Show the small fire or the calm room, and skip the alarm. Red alert screens, countdown timers, sirens and skulls have no place here, even as a joke in an engineering post.

"}, {"ref": "source_145", "relative_path": "brand/channels/blog-playbook.md", "heading_path": ["Writing for the Wickhold blog", "2. The intro"], "start_line": 13, "end_line": 36, "content": "## 2. The intro

A blog intro must cite a market statistic. Put it in the first two sentences, in the citation format from the style guide, and follow it with one sentence that says why this post exists. The rule is there because engineers are more willing to keep reading once they know the problem is measured and someone has measured it honestly.

Statistics are subject to the age limit in the approved claims, so check the date before you reuse an intro from an older post.

Market statistics are figures about the market or a surveyed population. Our own customer results and benchmark numbers belong further down the post, and they don't satisfy this requirement.

Good:

> The median time to contain a runtime incident is 7.4 hours [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report]. Most of the teams we talk to can tell you how long detection took. Far fewer can tell you what happened in the hours after. This post is about those hours.

Good:

> 41% of platform teams need more than six hours to contain a runtime incident [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report]. A lot of that time goes to one question: who is allowed to touch the workload? Here is how to settle that question before the page goes off.

Bad, because it has no statistic and no reason to read on:

> Kubernetes has changed how modern teams ship software, and with that change come new security challenges.

Bad, because a customer result is doing the job of a market statistic:

> Lowmoor Credit Union cut time to contain from 4 hours to 11 minutes. Here's how your team can get the same results.

"}, {"ref": "source_146", "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md", "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "15. Usage notes"], "start_line": 224, "end_line": 245, "content": "## 15. Usage notes

- **a/an:** go by sound. An eBPF agent, a SOC 2 report, an SRE.
- **back end** (noun), **back-end** (adjective).
- **cyber:** avoid as a prefix. Say what kind of security you mean.
- **data** is singular in our copy: "the data is".
- **drain:** a verb in Kubernetes and in our copy. "Drained the node."
- **e.g., i.e., etc.:** write "for example", "that is", or finish the list.
- **email:** no hyphen.
- **failover** (noun), **fail over** (verb).
- **in order to:** "to".
- **log in** (verb), **login** (noun). Same pattern for **set up / setup**, **roll out / rollout**, **shut down / shutdown**.
- **real time** (noun), **real-time** (adjective).
- **sidecar, service mesh:** lowercase, one and two words.
- **startup:** one word.
- **third party** (noun), **third-party** (adjective).
- **trade-off:** hyphenated.
- **utilize:** "use".
- **very, really, extremely:** delete and reread.
- **via:** "through", unless it's a technical path.
- **zero-day:** hyphenated, and only for an actual zero-day.

"}, {"ref": "source_147", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "4. Positioning", "The brand idea"], "start_line": 124, "end_line": 129, "content": "### The brand idea

A wick is where a fire is allowed to exist. It gives the flame a place to be, and it keeps the flame there. That is the idea behind the name, the mark and the tagline. Wickhold accepts that production systems have heat in them. The job is to hold it to a small, known place.

This idea should explain design and copy decisions when a rule doesn't. When two options are both on brand, pick the one that feels calmer and more contained.

"}, {"ref": "source_148", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "11. Governance", "Owners"], "start_line": 484, "end_line": 493, "content": "### Owners

"}, {"ref": "source_149", "relative_path": "brand/voice/voice-and-tone-2026.md", "heading_path": ["Wickhold voice and tone", "Before you send it for review"], "start_line": 272, "end_line": 284, "content": "## Before you send it for review

Read it out loud as a handover to the next on-call. If you stumble, or feel you are selling to a colleague, rewrite that part.

Then a few checks that catch most problems:

- Can a stranger tell what happened, what is contained and what is next?
- Does each claim have a figure and a source, or is it a plain description of what the product does?
- Is there an "I" or "we think" outside a signed founder piece?
- Does anything rely on the reader being scared?
- What's the last line doing there?

Copy review goes through #brand-review, and Noor or one of the brand team turns it around in two working days. Claims go to Priit Salonen's team and take the time the approved claims set. If a deadline leans on either of those, say so early.
"}, {"ref": "source_150", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/by-content-type/blog-hero.md", "heading_path": ["Blog hero images"], "start_line": 1, "end_line": 8, "content": "# Blog hero images

Content team working rules, June 2026.

"}, {"ref": "source_151", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "9. Photography and illustration direction", "Choosing between them"], "start_line": 424, "end_line": 433, "content": "### Choosing between them

| If the piece is about | Lean toward |
|---|---|
| People, customers, the company | Photography |
| An idea or a risk | Illustration |
| What the product does | Product imagery |

Security imagery has a set of tired visual habits, and the brand stays well clear of them. Fear is not part of the visual language, for the same reason it is not part of the verbal one.

"}, {"ref": "source_152", "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md", "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "4. Numbers", "Money"], "start_line": 93, "end_line": 98, "content": "### Money

- Dollars with the symbol: $18, $29. No ".00".
- Node pricing is written in full: "$18 per node per month". Not "/node/mo", not "per-node", not "$18 pnpm", which someone did actually write in a deck.
- Funding and other large sums use a capital M and no space: $46M. Don't write "$46 million" in one place and "$46M" in another; pick the M.

"}, {"ref": "source_161", "relative_path": "brand/archive/landing/quenchline-landing-current.md", "heading_path": ["Runtime containment for Kubernetes, decided before the incident", "The numbers"], "start_line": 42, "end_line": 47, "content": "## The numbers

"}, {"ref": "source_162", "relative_path": "brand/archive/blog/comparison-quenchline-vs-tesserline-2026.md", "heading_path": ["Comparison: Wickhold Quenchline and Tesserline for runtime containment", "Where Quenchline is the better choice"], "start_line": 27, "end_line": 34, "content": "## Where Quenchline is the better choice

Containment is the difference. When Tesserline detects something, a person or another tool has to do the next step. When Quenchline detects something covered by your default containment policy, it can take the containment action itself. For a team with a small on-call rotation and no staffed night shift, that gap accounts for much of the time described in the report: the alert fires, then someone wakes up, finds the owner, and gets permission.

In Wickhold lab benchmarks, 2026, Quenchline contains a known-bad process in a median of 38 seconds. That is a lab figure, and it includes no human approval by design. Lowmoor Credit Union, running Quenchline on 220 nodes, saw time to contain fall from 4 hours to 11 minutes. That is one customer's result on one estate, and yours will depend on how much you are willing to automate.

Rule maintenance is the other practical difference. A big rule library has to be tuned, and tuning is real work. Teams without a detection engineer tend to end up muting rules, and a muted rule detects nothing. Quenchline's smaller rule set leaves less to tune, at the cost of less control.

"}, {"ref": "source_163", "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md", "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "1. Headlines"], "start_line": 14, "end_line": 35, "content": "## 1. Headlines

**Headlines are in sentence case.** Capitalize the first word and any proper noun. Everything else is lowercase.

This covers page titles, blog titles, section headings, email subject lines, slide titles, buttons, nav labels, form labels, table headers and any text set over an image. If it looks like a heading, it is one.

| Right | Wrong |
|---|---|
| What contain mode does to a running pod | What Contain Mode Does To A Running Pod |
| Wickhold Containment Report 2026 | WICKHOLD CONTAINMENT REPORT 2026 |
| How Ostler Grocers cut its open critical misconfigurations | How Ostler Grocers Cut Its Open Critical Misconfigurations |

Details:

- Product names, event names and the report title keep their capitals, as do Kubernetes, Helm, CVE and the rest of the proper vocabulary. `containerd` and `eBPF` keep their lowercase starts even as the first word, though it's nicer to rewrite so that neither opens a headline.
- The word after a colon is lowercase: "Drift: what it is and how to read it".
- No full stop on headlines. The tagline is the one exception, and it keeps its full stop everywhere.
- No code formatting in headlines. They break in email clients and in link previews.
- Keep a headline to one idea. If it needs a colon and a dash, it's two headlines.

The old sheet used Title Case for everything over 24px. That went in the rebrand, and pages still carrying it get fixed when someone next touches them.

"}, {"ref": "source_166", "relative_path": "brand/voice/voice-and-tone-2026.md", "heading_path": ["Wickhold voice and tone", "What Wickhold believes", "Say the number, then stop"], "start_line": 61, "end_line": 76, "content": "### Say the number, then stop

Claims carry a figure and a source. No adjective stacks.

"Fast" is not a claim. "A fast, powerful, highly scalable runtime platform" is three non-claims in a row. Write the number, say where it came from, and end the sentence. The urge to add a second sentence explaining why the number is impressive is the urge to resist. A reader who needs that sentence is the wrong reader; a reader who doesn't will think less of us for it.

Bad: "Lowmoor Credit Union saw an incredible, game-changing reduction in response times."

Good: "Lowmoor Credit Union cut time to contain from 4 hours to 11 minutes across 220 nodes."

Bad: "Quenchline is extremely lightweight and blazingly quick."

Good: "Wickhold Quenchline contains a known-bad process in a median of 38 seconds in Wickhold lab benchmarks, 2026."

If there is no figure, there is usually no claim, and the honest move is to describe what the product does in plain mechanical terms. "Isolates a pod's network" needs no number and no source. It's a description. "Industry-leading isolation" needs both and has neither.

"}, {"ref": "source_172", "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md", "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "6. Grammar and punctuation"], "start_line": 115, "end_line": 132, "content": "## 6. Grammar and punctuation

- **American spelling** in all copy, including copy going to UK and EU readers. Containerize, not containerise.
- **Oxford comma**, always. It has settled more than one argument in Kubernetes prose, where lists of nouns can double as lists of objects.
- **Active voice** with a named actor, wherever the actor is known. "Wickhold Quenchline drained the node." If the passive is hiding who did it and that person is us, it goes.
- **Tense.** Past for what happened, present for what the product does, and nothing in the future except where a date is public.
- **Contractions** are fine in the blog, on social and in email. Skip them on legal pages and in anything aimed at a board.
- **Colons** are our favorite punctuation mark and they're doing fine. Use them to introduce the fact.
- **Semicolons** at most once a page. If there are two, one wants to be a full stop.
- **Em dashes** rarely in body copy. Most are a full stop that lost its nerve. Spaced en dashes are not a substitute.
- **Parentheses** for the short aside only. If the aside matters, promote it to a sentence.
- **Quotation marks:** double, with commas and full stops inside, American style, except for literal strings in technical writing where the punctuation would change the meaning. Single quotes only inside double.
- **Italics:** titles of reports and the occasional stress only. They disappear on Soot grounds and in email.
- **Bold:** for scanning in long documents, once or twice per section. Bold on a landing page means the design isn't working.
- **Ampersands:** only in proper names. Plain "and" in headlines too.
- **"And/or"** is a legal term. Pick one.
- **Slashes** as a shortcut ("platform/security teams") get rewritten: "platform and security teams".

"}, {"ref": "source_173", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "4. Positioning", "Positioning statement"], "start_line": 138, "end_line": 143, "content": "### Positioning statement

"}, {"ref": "source_174", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/by-content-type/linkedin-image.md", "heading_path": ["LinkedIn images", "Document posts and video"], "start_line": 45, "end_line": 48, "content": "## Document posts and video

"}, {"ref": "source_175", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/00-visual-rules-common.md", "heading_path": ["Visual rules common to every image", "The two rules that come up every week", "One focal point"], "start_line": 37, "end_line": 48, "content": "### One focal point

Every image has one focal point. A reader should be able to say what the image is of after a second's look. If two things compete, crop or pick another image.

Tests we use in review:

- Squint at it. One shape or area should hold.
- Shrink it to a thumbnail. Something should still be identifiable.
- Describe it in one short sentence without "and". "An engineer reading a terminal in a dark room" passes. "A team at a table and a wall of monitors and a logo on the door" does not.

Collages, split screens and before-and-after pairs fail this unless they are charts, where the comparison is the single point.

"}, {"ref": "source_176", "relative_path": "brand/legal/approved-claims-2026.md", "heading_path": ["Approved claims, 2026", "4. Certification status"], "start_line": 99, "end_line": 104, "content": "## 4. Certification status

"}, {"ref": "source_177", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/accessibility.md", "heading_path": ["Image accessibility", "Alt text on every image"], "start_line": 5, "end_line": 24, "content": "## Alt text on every image

Every image has alt text. This covers blog images, email images, landing pages, social uploads where the platform offers the field, and images in PDFs. The author of the piece writes it, because the designer usually does not know why the image is there.

Write what the reader would lose if the image failed to load. One or two plain sentences, under about 125 characters when you can manage it. Skip "image of" and "picture of". Do not stuff keywords. Do not paste the `description` field from the library: that describes the file, and alt text describes what the image is doing in this piece.

| Image | Bad | Good |
|---|---|---|
| Photo | "Engineer, Kubernetes, security, on-call, data center" | "An engineer reads a terminal in a dim equipment room." |
| Product screenshot | "Screenshot of dashboard" | "Quenchline shows one pod isolated, with network access removed and the process frozen." |
| Chart | "Bar chart" | "Median time to contain a runtime incident is 7.4 hours. Wickhold Containment Report 2026." |
| Logo | "logo.png" | "Wickhold logo" |
| Illustration | "Decorative graphic" | "A cut-paper wick with a single small Ember flame." |

Charts and screenshots carry the finding in the alt text, and the reader should not need the picture to get the number. If the chart has more than about four values, put the values in a table or the body copy under it and let the alt text state the point.

Any text set on an image must also appear in the alt text or the surrounding copy. Screen readers cannot read a stat card.

The "every image" part holds for decorative images too. If an image truly adds nothing, the first question is why it is in the piece. Background textures set in CSS are not images for this purpose and need no alt.

"}, {"ref": "source_180", "relative_path": "brand/voice/voice-and-tone-2026.md", "heading_path": ["Wickhold voice and tone", "Reading old copy"], "start_line": 257, "end_line": 262, "content": "## Reading old copy

Pre-2026 material is everywhere: the archive, old decks, the sales team's memory. It sounds different for a reason. The old brand sold watching. It leaned on "always", "every" and "complete", and it got excited in public. A lot of it is competent copy for a company we no longer are.

"}, {"ref": "source_181", "relative_path": "brand/legal/approved-claims-2026.md", "heading_path": ["Approved claims, 2026", "5. Statistics: 12-month age limit"], "start_line": 105, "end_line": 126, "content": "## 5. Statistics: 12-month age limit

A market statistic may not be older than 12 months at publication. This is the limit on how old a statistic can be, and it is measured on the day the piece goes out, not the day it was drafted. A post queued in March for release in May is checked against May.

The limit applies to market and survey statistics only. It covers any figure that describes the industry, the market, or a population of teams. It does not apply to customer results such as the Lowmoor and Ostler outcomes, or to product metrics such as the lab figures, which have their own qualifier.

The age of a statistic runs from the publication date of its source. Fieldwork dates do not matter. A report re-quoted in a newer article keeps its original date, so a 2026 article quoting a 2024 survey is a 2024 statistic.

Applied to our own reports:

| Source | Published | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Wickhold Containment Report 2026 | April 14, 2026 | Usable for publication through April 14, 2027 |
| Wickhold Field Report 2024 | 2024 | Past the 12 months limit |
| Wickhold Field Report 2023 | 2023 | Past the 12 months limit |

The two Containment Report statistics in section 1 are the only market statistics of ours inside the limit today. The Field Report figures still appear in old decks and old posts. That is an archive problem and not a permission. Do not reuse them. Do not reword them to make them feel new, and do not refer to them as "historically" true.

Fresh third-party statistics are allowed without coming to me first, with the source link and the date of the source in the copy. The source must be a named publisher and the figure must appear on the page you link to. A figure found in a vendor's blog, quoting another vendor's blog, gets traced to the original or is dropped. The third party's name still has to clear the competitor rules.

When the 2027 Containment Report is published, section 1 will be updated and the 2026 figures remain usable until they reach the limit. Old assets stay in the archive as they are. They are not re-promoted once a market statistic in them has expired. Paid and email reuse counts as publication.

"}, {"ref": "source_182", "relative_path": "brand/legal/regional-rules-eu-uk.md", "heading_path": ["Regional rules: EU and UK copy"], "start_line": 1, "end_line": 6, "content": "## Regional rules: EU and UK copy

Priit Salonen, with notes from the field marketing review, August 2026

Applies to anything aimed at readers in the EU or the UK: campaigns, event pages, email sends, localized landing pages, press outreach, partner co-marketing. If a global asset will run in those regions, it is regional copy too.

"}, {"ref": "source_183", "relative_path": "brand/templates/email-templates.md", "heading_path": ["Email templates", "CTA format for all channels"], "start_line": 7, "end_line": 22, "content": "## CTA format for all channels

This lives here because the email team wrote it down first, and it now applies to every channel: email, landing pages, paid, social, the blog, event pages.

A CTA, the call to action on a button or a link, is at most four words, and it starts with a verb. The same CTA wording rules apply wherever the button sits. "Learn more" and "Click here" are banned everywhere, including as link text inside a sentence.

| Fine | Not fine |
|---|---|
| Read the report | Learn more |
| Book a demo | Click here |
| See the rollout guide | Click here to see the rollout guide |
| Request early access | Early access request |
| Save your seat | Your seat is waiting for you |

Say what happens on the other side of the click. "Get started" is allowed but weak, so use something more specific if you can.

"}, {"ref": "source_184", "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md", "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "10. Links"], "start_line": 187, "end_line": 192, "content": "## 10. Links

"}, {"ref": "source_185", "relative_path": "brand/legal/customer-logo-and-quote-policy.md", "heading_path": ["Customer logo and quote policy", "Not cleared"], "start_line": 20, "end_line": 25, "content": "## Not cleared

**Vaskell Health is not cleared.** Do not use the name, logo, people, quotes or results in anything external, and do not use them in a customer-facing deck. "A large health system" does not help, because the draft material is specific enough to identify them. The draft case study in the folder stays a draft. No approval was given, and a finished-looking layout does not change that.

Everyone else is not cleared by default. Companies seen in a contract, in a support ticket, or in a Slow Burn Summit attendee list are not references.

"}, {"ref": "source_186", "relative_path": "brand/voice/voice-and-tone-2026.md", "heading_path": ["Wickhold voice and tone", "The character"], "start_line": 18, "end_line": 36, "content": "## The character

Wickhold is someone who has been paged more often than you have and is not going to bring it up.

**Unhurried.** Nothing in our copy is urgent. A page that hurries the reader is using the same trick as the alert fatigue they came to us to get away from.

**Exact.** "Isolated the pod's network" beats "took action". "220 nodes" beats "at scale". If two engineers would argue over what a sentence means, it isn't finished.

**Unimpressed by itself.** The product is useful. Copy that gasps at it reads as though the writer has not seen it fail. We have seen it fail, and the release notes say so.

**On your side of the pager.** The reader is a peer on the same rota, and we write to them as someone who could take the next shift. No lecturing, no "did you know", no explaining Kubernetes to people who run it.

When the character slips, it usually slips into one of four people:

- **The hero.** Rushes in, saves the day, gets the credit. Early rebrand drafts leaned on firefighters and helmets until Maren pointed out that a firefighter arriving means it already went badly. The customer's on-call team is the competent party in every story we tell.
- **The prophet.** Sees doom everywhere and sells shelter from it. The whole security industry's default register, which makes it invisible to the people we want to reach.
- **The buddy.** "Hey there, Kubernetes friends." Nobody paged at 3am wants a pal.
- **The analyst.** "In today's rapidly evolving threat landscape." Sentences with no one in them. If nothing would change when the paragraph is deleted, delete it.

"}, {"ref": "source_187", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "11. Governance", "Raising a conflict"], "start_line": 519, "end_line": 528, "content": "### Raising a conflict

If two documents disagree, don't quietly pick one and move on, because the next person will hit the same thing. Follow the order of authority for the piece in hand, ship it, and then send a short note to the owner of the lower document.

A useful note says three things and takes a minute to write:

> "These two documents give different answers on the same point. I used the higher one. Can the other be updated?"

The owner corrects the lower document or explains why it stands. If the higher document is the one that's out of date, the owner of that document changes it. Nobody overrides it locally.

"}, {"ref": "source_188", "relative_path": "brand/legal/approved-claims-2026.md", "heading_path": ["Approved claims, 2026", "8. Spoken claims, demos and records"], "start_line": 170, "end_line": 177, "content": "## 8. Spoken claims, demos and records

Spoken claims count. A webinar is a publication, a sales call can end up quoted in a procurement file, and a recorded conference talk stays available for years. Speakers get the same tables as writers. Questions from the floor that go beyond them are answered with "I will get back to you", and then with an email to me.

Demo environments show synthetic data. A demo may show a containment action in contain mode, and the timing shown on screen is not a claim about customer environments. Presenters should say so if anyone asks. Screenshots from a real customer tenant are not used in any circumstance.

The owner of each asset keeps the published version, or a link to it, and the source for each figure in it for three years. When a claim is withdrawn I will send a list of the assets I know about. I do not know about all of them, so owners should search their own material.

"}, {"ref": "source_189", "relative_path": "brand/channels/blog-playbook.md", "heading_path": ["Writing for the Wickhold blog", "9. Updating old posts"], "start_line": 118, "end_line": 123, "content": "## 9. Updating old posts

Older posts stay up, but they can mislead. The brand team runs through the top 30 posts by traffic every quarter. Each gets one of three outcomes: leave it, edit it in place with an "Updated" date at the top, or redirect it to a newer post.

Edit in place when a product name, a command or a figure has gone out of date. Redirect when the advice has changed. Never quietly change a claim. If a post said something that turned out to be wrong, add a line saying what changed and when. Engineers notice, and they remember how you handled it.

"}, {"ref": "source_190", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "9. Photography and illustration direction", "Product imagery"], "start_line": 403, "end_line": 406, "content": "### Product imagery

Screenshots and diagrams show the real product and real terms. When a choice exists between a clever visual metaphor and a clear view of what the product did, show the product.

"}, {"ref": "source_191", "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md", "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "4. Numbers", "Percentages"], "start_line": 73, "end_line": 81, "content": "### Percentages

**Percentages use digits and the % symbol.** Always, including at the start of a sentence, in headlines, in legal-reviewed copy and in speech written for a stage.

- Right: 41% of platform teams, 63% fewer open critical misconfigurations.
- Wrong: forty-one percent, 41 percent, 41 per cent, 63pc.

No space before the symbol. "Percentage points" is written out when you mean the difference between two percentages, and it's rare enough in our copy that a reviewer will ask if you're sure.

"}, {"ref": "source_192", "relative_path": "brand/legal/approved-claims-2026.md", "heading_path": ["Approved claims, 2026", "2. Claims that need a qualifier", "Wickhold Leashgate (early access)"], "start_line": 73, "end_line": 78, "content": "### Wickhold Leashgate (early access)

Leashgate is in early access. Claims describe what the early access product does today. They do not describe a roadmap, and they do not give a date.

Permitted vocabulary is tool-call policy, agent identity, and the blast radius of an agent. The approved outcome statement is "limits what a compromised agent can do".

"}, {"ref": "source_193", "relative_path": "brand/legal/approved-claims-2026.md", "heading_path": ["Approved claims, 2026", "2. Claims that need a qualifier", "Market statistics"], "start_line": 59, "end_line": 62, "content": "### Market statistics

Name the source and the year each time. A market statistic in a headline needs its source on the same screen or page section. See section 5 for how long a statistic stays usable.

"}, {"ref": "source_194", "relative_path": "brand/legal/customer-logo-and-quote-policy.md", "heading_path": ["Customer logo and quote policy", "Anonymous examples"], "start_line": 26, "end_line": 29, "content": "## Anonymous examples

"}, {"ref": "source_196", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "1. What changed in 2026", "Why the company rebranded"], "start_line": 11, "end_line": 16, "content": "### Why the company rebranded

The 2024 brand made a promise about watching. It suited a company that sold visibility, and it stopped fitting as the product moved on. By 2025 the feature customers talked about in renewals was the moment Wickhold Quenchline isolated a pod's network at 3am and nobody had to get out of bed. Sales calls kept going the same way: the prospect would say every tool they owned could see a problem, and then ask what happens next.

Ilse Varga-Holm, who owns the rebrand, started the work in spring 2025 with a set of about 30 customer and on-call interviews. Maren Tolliver and Dov Achterberg sat in on most of them. The clearest finding was that nobody wanted another thing watching them. They wanted the blast of an incident to be smaller and the morning after to be shorter. That finding drove every decision below.

"}, {"ref": "source_197", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "7. Color", "Mistakes seen since launch"], "start_line": 323, "end_line": 326, "content": "### Mistakes seen since launch

The single most common mistake since launch is treating Ember as the "main" color because the table calls it primary. Primary means most important, and it does not mean most area.

"}, {"ref": "source_198", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/by-content-type/blog-hero.md", "heading_path": ["Blog hero images", "Size and crop"], "start_line": 24, "end_line": 29, "content": "## Size and crop

Export at 1600x900. Most library heroes and photos are 3:2, so you will lose some height. Crop from the top and bottom, then check that the focal point has survived. A hero illustration's focal element usually sits off center and the quiet part can go. Some platforms crop preview cards further, so keep the focal point out of the outer tenth of the frame.

Do not upscale. A 1536-wide source enlarged to 1600 is about the limit, and it should look clean at full size.

"}, {"ref": "source_199", "relative_path": "brand/legal/approved-claims-2026.md", "heading_path": ["Approved claims, 2026", "2. Claims that need a qualifier", "Lab figures"], "start_line": 36, "end_line": 58, "content": "### Lab figures

Two product figures come from Wickhold's own lab. Both must carry the phrase "in Wickhold lab benchmarks, 2026", in the same sentence as the figure.

| Figure | Required form |
|---|---|
| CPU overhead | "under 2% CPU overhead on a typical node in Wickhold lab benchmarks, 2026" |
| Containment speed | "contains a known-bad process in a median of 38 seconds in Wickhold lab benchmarks, 2026" |

A footnote does not meet this requirement. An asterisk does not meet it. A qualifier on the slide before does not meet it. In a chart, the phrase goes in the chart title or directly under it. In a talk, the speaker says it aloud.

The figures describe a lab, so they may not be presented as field results or customer averages. "Known-bad process" is part of the claim: it does not extend to unknown processes, novel techniques, or "threats" in general. Reports may repeat the figures only if the benchmark year stays attached. When the 2027 benchmarks run, the year changes and this table is reissued. Nobody edits the year by hand.

Approved:

> Wickhold Quenchline adds under 2% CPU overhead on a typical node in Wickhold lab benchmarks, 2026.

Not approved:

> Quenchline contains attacks in 38 seconds.

> Under 2% overhead. Guaranteed.

Something will get through. Every serious engineer already knows this, and the companies who claim otherwise are talking to someone else. "}, {"ref": "source_206", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/00-visual-rules-common.md", "heading_path": ["Visual rules common to every image", "The two rules that come up every week", "No generated text in any image"], "start_line": 23, "end_line": 36, "content": "### No generated text in any image

No image contains text produced by an image model or baked into artwork by a tool that does not treat it as live type. Models misspell product names, invent letterforms and produce near-English that survives one quick look and then gets screenshotted by a customer. We had a test hero in spring where a wall sign read almost like "Quenchline". Nobody caught it until it was in a review deck.

Text in a Wickhold image is set by a person, in the design tool, in the brand typefaces, as a separate layer over finished art. That covers overlays, labels, chart annotations and callouts.

Three things do not count as generated text:

- Words that are really in the scene: a printed rack label, a whiteboard someone wrote on, a door sign. Check that they say nothing embarrassing and name nobody outside the company.
- Real interface text in a true product screenshot.
- The wordmark, which is a vector file, placed by a person.

Some placements allow no overlay at all and others cap it. The content-type page has the number.

"}, {"ref": "source_207", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "4. Positioning", "Tagline"], "start_line": 130, "end_line": 137, "content": "### Tagline

The current tagline is **Small fires stay small.**

It is written with sentence case and a full stop, and the full stop is part of it. Do not vary it, translate it into a campaign pun, or extend it with a second clause. It can stand alone under the logo, close a piece, or sit at the end of a deck. It does not need to appear in every piece, and one use per piece is the limit.

If the library has nothing suitable, do not borrow from the web, do not pull an image from a past deck, and do not take it from a teammate's desktop. Files outside the library have no record and nobody can check their rights.

Requests go to the brand designers through the design queue with the placement, the deadline and one sentence on what the image should show. Allow five working days for illustration and more for photography that needs a shoot. Anything made for you gets a metadata record before it ships.

"}, {"ref": "source_209", "relative_path": "brand/legal/approved-claims-2026.md", "heading_path": ["Approved claims, 2026", "1. Claims approved as written", "Customer count"], "start_line": 28, "end_line": 33, "content": "### Customer count

The only approved claim is "more than 140 customers". The following are not approved: "140+ customers", "nearly 150 customers", "hundreds of customers", "thousands of engineers", or any count of nodes, clusters or workloads summed across the customer base. Finance reconciles the number each quarter against active contracts. Pilots, lapsed accounts, open-source users, and companies that attended Slow Burn Summit are not customers for this purpose.

When the reconciled number supports a higher claim, this document will change. Until it does, the number in a sales deck, a conference bio or a partner page is the number here. If you have seen a larger figure in circulation, it is wrong, and I would like to know where you saw it.

"}, {"ref": "source_214", "relative_path": "brand/channels/linkedin-playbook.md", "heading_path": ["LinkedIn playbook", "Format"], "start_line": 17, "end_line": 26, "content": "## Format

- A LinkedIn post is 180 words at most. Count everything, including the link line.
- About the first 200 characters show before the "see more" cut on most phones. The news has to fit in that space.
- Short paragraphs, one to three lines each, with a blank line between them.
- One link per post, at the end, on its own line. We tested putting links in the first comment for six weeks in 2025 and could not see a difference, and it annoyed people, so links stay in the post.
- Tag a customer only after their marketing contact has seen the post. Tag people, not company pages, when a named person spoke or wrote the thing.
- Use bullets only for real lists: three containment actions, the tiers, the steps of a rollout. A post that is all bullets reads as a slide.
- Image guidance sits with the visual rules. Every company page post gets one image, except short hiring notes.

"}, {"ref": "source_218", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/00-visual-rules-common.md", "heading_path": ["Visual rules common to every image", "The image library and its metadata", "restrictions: check it before every use"], "start_line": 82, "end_line": 97, "content": "### `restrictions`: check it before every use

Read `restrictions` before you use an image, every time, including images you have used before. Restrictions are added after an image enters the library, so last quarter's check does not count.

The field is free text, written by whoever had the reason. There is no fixed vocabulary, so read the sentence instead of searching for a keyword. Three kinds of note turn up in practice:

- **Retirement.** The image is deprecated and must not be used. Some retired files look entirely normal in the grid and carry no other sign. Their tags and titles may even look current.
- **A limited context.** The image may be used in the named context and nowhere else. A note limiting an image to internal use keeps it out of anything a customer, a prospect or the press will see, and that includes sales decks.
- **A person or place.** Something about who or what is shown has changed.

A restriction binds even when the image would be perfect, when a senior person asks for it, and when you found it already published somewhere. If you think one is out of date, ask Brand to change the record. Do not use the image and sort it out later.

An empty `restrictions` field means nobody has recorded a limit. It does not mean the image is on brand. The field is one check among several, and the current-identity rule above still has to pass on your own judgment.

If `restrictions` and `tags` seem to disagree, `restrictions` wins. If `restrictions` and `description` disagree, stop and ask.

"}, {"ref": "source_219", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "11. Governance", "Worked examples"], "start_line": 468, "end_line": 483, "content": "### Worked examples

**Two limits for the same channel.** A general voice document gives one length for a channel and that channel's playbook gives another. The playbook wins, because it sits higher in the list. Use its number, and tell Noor so the other one gets fixed.

**A claim in a deck.** A slide says something about the company that the approved claims do not support. The approved claims win, however recent or confident the slide looks, and however often the line has been used in the field. Sales material is not a source for a claim.

**Copy in this document versus Legal.** If a sentence in these guidelines turns out to conflict with the approved claims, Legal wins, and the guidelines get corrected.

**An old-looking rule with no rival.** A meeting note from the Q2 brand review covers something that the relevant playbook doesn't mention. Nothing conflicts, so the note stands.

**A file that says it's the latest.** File names, version numbers and words like FINAL or CURRENT decide nothing. Neither does the date on a file, on its own. Use this list.

**No source answers the question.** Ask the owner listed below. Do not fill the gap from the 2024 material or from what a competitor does. If the question is likely to come up again, the answer gets written down in the right document.

**Sources at the same level disagree.** Two channel playbooks can conflict on a shared element, such as a campaign running on both email and a landing page. Each playbook governs its own channel. If that doesn't settle it, Noor decides and the decision gets recorded.

"}, {"ref": "source_220", "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md", "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "11. Tables, charts and captions"], "start_line": 193, "end_line": 201, "content": "## 11. Tables, charts and captions

- A table needs a header row and at least two rows of content. One row is a sentence.
- Right-align numbers in tables. Keep units in the header, not in each cell.
- A chart title states the finding in sentence case: "41% of platform teams need more than six hours to contain a runtime incident". The axis says what was measured.
- Every chart carries its citation in the same bracket form, set small under the chart, so it survives being cropped into a slide.
- Captions are sentences. They end with a full stop and they don't begin "Figure 1 shows".
- No 3D, no donuts, and no chart for a single number. Write the number.

"}, {"ref": "source_221", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "4. Positioning", "The market problem"], "start_line": 144, "end_line": 149, "content": "### The market problem

The strongest evidence for this position comes from Wickhold's own research. The Wickhold Containment Report 2026, published April 14, 2026, surveyed 412 platform and security leaders. It found that "41% of platform teams need more than six hours to contain a runtime incident" and that "the median time to contain a runtime incident is 7.4 hours" [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report].

The gap those numbers describe is between finding something and doing something about it. Detection has become cheap and common. Containment still depends on a person with enough access waking up, reading the alert, deciding, and acting. Wickhold's position lives in those hours.

"}, {"ref": "source_222", "relative_path": "brand/templates/email-templates.md", "heading_path": ["Email templates", "T6. Nurture, platform track, first email"], "start_line": 142, "end_line": 160, "content": "## T6. Nurture, platform track, first email
