"}, {"ref": "source_223", "relative_path": "brand/voice/word-list.md", "heading_path": ["Word list", "Not banned, but expect a comment"], "start_line": 39, "end_line": 52, "content": "## Not banned, but expect a comment

Reviewers will ask about these. Sometimes the word survives.

- **solution.** Name the product, or say what it does. The word exists to avoid doing either.
- **visibility.** Seeing isn't the job. If the sentence ends at seeing, ask what happens next.
- **real-time.** Fine with a number next to it. Without one it means nothing.
- **AI-powered.** Tells the reader how something was built and nothing about what it does.
- **comprehensive.** Usually untrue, and a reader will go looking for the gap.
- **threat landscape.** A landscape has no one in it. Say which failure you mean.
- **peace of mind.** Nobody on a rota has ever had this.
- **modern.** Compared with what? Say which setup you mean.
- **mission-critical.** To the person on call, everything is.

"}, {"ref": "source_224", "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md", "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "5. Dates and times"], "start_line": 103, "end_line": 114, "content": "## 5. Dates and times

- **Dates:** month, day, year, spelled out: April 14, 2026. No ordinals, no "14th of April".
- **Month and year:** March 2022, no comma. **Year only:** 2026.
- **Ranges:** an en dash with no spaces within a month: September 15–16. Use "to" across months: "March 30 to April 2".
- **Tables, logs, front matter:** ISO, 2026-04-14. Never slashes. 04/10 has already caused one wrong webinar invite, and that's enough.
- **Quarters:** fine internally. In public copy, name the month.
- **Avoid relative dates** in anything that stays online. "Recently", "last year", "this spring" and "soon" all rot. Write the date. Press releases and dated posts can say "today".
- **Roadmap language:** no dates, no "coming soon". Product marketing has a separate process for that.

**Times.** Incident timelines use 24-hour UTC with the zone on every line or at the top of the block: 03:14 UTC. It's how our readers' tools show it. Event and webinar times use 12-hour with the zone: 2:00 p.m. MT. In prose, "3am" with no space is fine as a phrase, and the voice document uses it constantly. It's a figure of speech and shouldn't be used for an actual appointment.

"}, {"ref": "source_225", "relative_path": "brand/channels/linkedin-playbook.md", "heading_path": ["LinkedIn playbook", "Who posts"], "start_line": 7, "end_line": 16, "content": "## Who posts

**Company page.** Marketing runs it. Two or three posts a week, Tuesday to Thursday, usually mid-morning Mountain time. Fridays stayed on the calendar through most of 2025 and did nothing, so they came off.

**Maren and Dov.** They post from their own profiles when they have something to say. Marketing can draft, but they rewrite. Do not schedule on their behalf without a yes in writing, and do not reply to comments as them. If a draft of Maren's has been sitting for two weeks, drop it. She has decided.

**Kofi and the DevRel team.** Kofi posts from his own profile about conference talks, open-source eBPF work and whatever broke in the demo cluster. He does not need brand review for those unless a post carries a customer name, a product claim or a number.

**Everyone else.** People can share company posts however they like. We ran an employee amplification program in 2025 with a shared doc of suggested captions. Forty people posted the same sentence on the same morning and it looked exactly like that. We stopped.

"}, {"ref": "source_226", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "5. Brand architecture", "Partners"], "start_line": 259, "end_line": 262, "content": "### Partners

Wickhold does not run a sub-brand for partners, resellers or integrations. A partner may say that it works with Wickhold, once the partner agreement is in place and Priit's team has reviewed the wording. There is no "Wickhold certified" badge, and there is no plan for one.

"}, {"ref": "source_227", "relative_path": "brand/archive/blog/comparison-quenchline-vs-tesserline-2026.md", "heading_path": ["Comparison: Wickhold Quenchline and Tesserline for runtime containment", "Short version"], "start_line": 9, "end_line": 20, "content": "## Short version

All Tesserline entries are as of its public documentation on July 14, 2026.

| | Wickhold Quenchline | Tesserline |
|---|---|---|
| Main job | Runtime detection and containment for Kubernetes | Runtime detection |
| Acts on what it finds | Yes: isolate a pod's network, freeze a process, drain a node | No built-in containment; alerts go to your tools |
| Detection approach | Behavior from an eBPF agent, plus a smaller rule set | Large rule library |
| Default posture on install | Observe mode, with contain mode set per policy | Alerting |
| Best fit | Teams who want decisions made in advance and executed by the tool | Teams with a staffed security operations function and their own response tooling |

"}, {"ref": "source_228", "relative_path": "brand/legal/approved-claims-2026.md", "heading_path": ["Approved claims, 2026", "7. Rulings from this year"], "start_line": 151, "end_line": 169, "content": "## 7. Rulings from this year

Requests I have already answered. They are listed so that I do not answer them again.

| Request | Ruling |
|---|---|
| "Trusted by more than 140 customers" | Allowed. The count stays exact |
| "Trusted by credit unions" | Refused. One customer is not a plural |
| "Agentless" or "agent-free" for Quenchline | Refused. It uses an eBPF agent. Say so |
| "Lightweight" | Allowed only next to the CPU overhead figure and its qualifier |
| "Real-time" for Quenchline | Allowed for detection. For containment, use the lab figure or leave it out |
| "Stops the attack" | Refused. Name the containment action: isolate a pod's network, freeze a process, drain a node |
| "Automatic remediation" for Evenburn | Refused. Evenburn gives a fix order and people do the fixing |
| "AI-powered" for any product | Refused unless product confirms in writing what the model does. Writing about AI agents does not make the product AI-powered |
| "Secures your AI" or "safe AI" for Leashgate | Refused. Describe tool-call policy and agent identity |
| "SOC 2 certified" | Refused. Say "holds SOC 2 Type II" |
| "Used by your peers" in a sector email | Refused unless a named, approved customer in that sector is shown |
| "Battle-tested" | Refused. It implies a history of incidents at customers that we have not disclosed and may not disclose |

"}, {"ref": "source_229", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "9. Photography and illustration direction", "Illustration"], "start_line": 395, "end_line": 402, "content": "### Illustration

Illustration is flat cut-paper shapes with one Ember focal element on Tallow or Soot, and no gradients. The cut-paper style was chosen because it looks made by hand and sits comfortably next to the warm photography. It also holds up small. Shapes should be simple enough to be cut with scissors, which is a good test when a design starts picking up detail.

Illustration tends to work best for ideas that have no honest photograph, such as a policy, a blast radius or an exposure path. Containment is the recurring theme: something small, held inside something that keeps it there.

The isometric style and the line graphic from the 2024 identity have been retired, along with the Cobalt gradient behind them.

"}, {"ref": "source_230", "relative_path": "brand/templates/email-templates.md", "heading_path": ["Email templates", "T8c. Renewal notice"], "start_line": 235, "end_line": 253, "content": "## T8c. Renewal notice

Owner: customer success. Sent 90 days before the renewal date, from the account's CSM.

**Subject:** Your Wickhold renewal on {{renewal_date}}
**Preheader:** Your current plan and node count, and who to talk to about changes.

Hi {{first_name}},

Your Wickhold subscription renews on {{renewal_date}}.

Current plan: {{tier}}. Nodes on contract: {{node_count}}.

If your node count has changed, or you'd like to look at adding Wickhold Evenburn, reply here and we'll go through it together. Otherwise there's nothing you need to do yet.

**[Review your plan]**

{{csm_first_name}}, Wickhold

"}, {"ref": "source_231", "relative_path": "brand/legal/regional-rules-eu-uk.md", "heading_path": ["Regional rules: EU and UK copy", "Analytics, cookies and tracking"], "start_line": 48, "end_line": 51, "content": "### Analytics, cookies and tracking

Localized landing pages use the consent banner supplied by web ops. Don't add a new tag, pixel or form tool to an EU or UK page without asking first. Paid retargeting on EU and UK traffic stays off unless the banner has recorded consent. A partner's tracking link is a new tag.

"}, {"ref": "source_232", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "11. Governance", "Agencies and freelancers"], "start_line": 509, "end_line": 512, "content": "### Agencies and freelancers

Outside partners work to the same order of authority, and the person who hired them is responsible for making sure they have it. At kickoff they receive these guidelines, the addendum, the relevant playbook and the current logo package. They do not receive older guidelines or old campaign files as reference, unless Brand has reviewed what's being sent. Work from outside partners goes through the same review table as anything made in-house.

"}, {"ref": "source_233", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "4. Positioning", "The promise at each level"], "start_line": 210, "end_line": 218, "content": "### The promise at each level

| Level | What is promised |
|---|---|
| Company | Small fires stay small. |
| Quenchline | When something goes wrong at runtime, a defined containment action happens quickly and the team sees exactly what it did |
| Evenburn | The team sees where the drift and exposure paths are, and gets a fix order |
| Leashgate | AI agents work inside a tool-call policy, so the blast radius of an agent is known in advance |

"}, {"ref": "source_234", "relative_path": "brand/legal/approved-claims-2026.md", "heading_path": ["Approved claims, 2026", "3. Banned claims"], "start_line": 79, "end_line": 98, "content": "## 3. Banned claims

| Do not say | Say instead, or do this | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| "prevents prompt injection" | "limits what a compromised agent can do" | Leashgate acts on tool calls. It does not read intent and it cannot promise that an agent will not be manipulated. The claim is false as a matter of product design |
| "FedRAMP Authorized", "FedRAMP certified" | See section 4 | Neither is true |
| "GDPR compliant" | Use the regional rules | Regional wording sits there, and the ban is not limited to that region |
| "breach-proof", "unhackable", "impossible to escape" | Describe the containment action | No security product can support an absolute |
| "zero false positives", "100% detection", "catches everything" | Give a sourced figure or say nothing | We hold no such evidence |
| "guarantee", "guaranteed", "warranty" outside a contract | Remove | These words have legal effect. Service credits live in the order form |
| "the leading", "the fastest", "No. 1", "the only" | Remove, or bring me the comparison data | Superlatives need current comparative substantiation, and we do not hold any |
| "certified by", "endorsed by", "partner of" for any standards body or open-source project | Remove | Using eBPF or Helm is not an endorsement from anyone |
| "saves $X", any return-on-investment figure | Remove | We have no approved financial outcome for any customer |

Two refinements, because they keep coming back:

"Helps prevent" is a banned claim dressed up. A qualifier in front of a promise does not make it a limited promise.

"Compliance-ready" and "audit-ready" were requested in June for a trust page and refused. Wickhold can describe what the product records. Whether a customer passes an audit depends on the customer and the auditor.

"}, {"ref": "source_235", "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md", "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "8. Technical writing in marketing copy"], "start_line": 143, "end_line": 153, "content": "## 8. Technical writing in marketing copy

Kofi Anselm's team reviews anything containing code, and their rules are short.

- **Code formatting** for commands, flags, file names, field names, namespaces, node names and anything a person might type: `kubectl get pods`, `--namespace`, `values.yaml`.
- **Every snippet is run before it's published.** Say which version it was run against. A snippet nobody ran does not go out, even in a slide.
- **Placeholder values** look like placeholders or like real workloads: `payments`, `checkout`, `worker-7`. Don't use `foo`, and don't use the name of a real company, a real customer or a celebrity.
- **Domains and email addresses in examples** use `wickhold.example`.
- **Long output** gets trimmed, with a line saying so. Don't silently edit output.
- **Failure modes** are part of the example. If a command fails in a common way, say how it looks.

"}, {"ref": "source_236", "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md", "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "4. Numbers"], "start_line": 71, "end_line": 72, "content": "## 4. Numbers

"}, {"ref": "source_237", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "7. Color", "Color in common pieces"], "start_line": 310, "end_line": 322, "content": "### Color in common pieces

| Piece | Ground | Where Ember goes |
|---|---|---|
| Website page | Tallow, with Soot bands for pacing | The primary button, or one key figure |
| Sales or conference deck | Soot for title and section slides, Tallow for content | One point on a slide, or none |
| Report | Tallow pages, Soot cover | Chart highlights and one rule on the cover |
| Product documentation | Follows the docs theme | Links are not Ember on small text |
| Booth | Soot backwall, Tallow counter | The dot in the logo and one line of type |
| Swag | Soot or undyed fabric | The dot |

Dark layouts should use Soot, and pure black should not stand in for it. Soot has a slight cool cast that keeps Ember from buzzing against it. On Tallow pages, photographs and screenshots sit best with a thin Whetstone rule around them, since a light screenshot can otherwise dissolve into the page.

"}, {"ref": "source_238", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "5. Brand architecture"], "start_line": 219, "end_line": 222, "content": "## 5. Brand architecture

Wickhold is a single brand. Products, reports and events all sit under it, and none of them has a logo of its own.

"}, {"ref": "source_239", "relative_path": "brand/voice/voice-and-tone-2026.md", "heading_path": ["Wickhold voice and tone", "What Wickhold believes", "Fear is not a sales tool"], "start_line": 41, "end_line": 56, "content": "### Fear is not a sales tool

No threat-actor drama. No ticking clocks.

The rule is simple to state and gets broken constantly, because fear copy is the easiest copy in security to write. It covers attackers portrayed as characters with motives and nicknames, anything of the "while you read this" kind, countdowns, "it's only a matter of time", "every second counts", and any sentence that asks the reader to imagine the phone call to the board. Our readers carry a pager. They do not need help imagining it.

Give the same fact without the dread.

Bad: "Attackers are already inside your cluster, and the clock is ticking."

Good: "41% of platform teams need more than six hours to contain a runtime incident [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report]."

The second sentence is more uncomfortable than the first, and it did not raise its voice. Trust the number to do that work.

Breach references have their own rules in the claims document. Read them before you mention one.

"}, {"ref": "source_240", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/by-content-type/linkedin-image.md", "heading_path": ["LinkedIn images", "What goes in the frame"], "start_line": 24, "end_line": 36, "content": "## What goes in the frame

Use, in rough order of how well they have done for us:

1. A photo of real work, with no overlay at all
2. A stat card from the social templates. Quote cards rarely fit the cap
3. A short product crop showing one action, large enough to read in the feed
4. A hero illustration, cropped

Library images are 3:2, so a 1200x627 crop loses about a fifth of the height. Keep the focal point near the vertical center. Spot illustrations should sit on a solid Tallow or Soot layout from the template. They are transparent and LinkedIn will show them on its own background if you upload them as they are.

Do not run overlay text across a photo's focal point. Text goes on a solid band or in the quiet side of the frame.

"}, {"ref": "source_241", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/by-content-type/blog-hero.md", "heading_path": ["Blog hero images", "Open graph card"], "start_line": 47, "end_line": 50, "content": "## Open graph card

The hero doubles as the social preview card unless a separate card is uploaded. Look at the preview before publishing, as the crop differs from the page. If the preview loses the focal point, upload a separate crop.

"}, {"ref": "source_242", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "7. Color", "Palette"], "start_line": 286, "end_line": 297, "content": "### Palette

| Name | Value | Role |
|---|---|---|
| Ember | `#C2501F` | Primary |
| Soot | `#15181C` | Ink |
| Tallow | `#F4EFE6` | Ground |
| Whetstone | `#5E6B73` | Secondary |
| Verdigris | `#2F8F83` | Secondary |

Precise color specifications, tints and measured contrast pairs are in the logo and color addendum.

"}, {"ref": "source_243", "relative_path": "brand/archive/landing/quenchline-landing-current.md", "heading_path": ["Runtime containment for Kubernetes, decided before the incident", "How it works"], "start_line": 26, "end_line": 33, "content": "## How it works

**Observe first.** The eBPF agent starts in observe mode and logs what it would have done. Most teams spend two to four weeks here, reading decision records.

**Write the policy.** Start from the default containment policy and decide which detection leads to which containment action. Policies go through your repo like any other change. Every exemption has an expiry date.

**Turn on contain mode where you are ready.** Mode is set per policy. Going back is one line.

"}, {"ref": "source_244", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/by-content-type/linkedin-image.md", "heading_path": ["LinkedIn images", "By account"], "start_line": 37, "end_line": 44, "content": "## By account

**Company page.** Follows all of the above. Logo present on designed images, absent on plain photos.

**Founder accounts.** Maren's and Dov's posts take a plain photo or no image. Designed cards with a company logo look like an ad under a personal post, so skip them. No overlay text on founder images unless Maren asks for it.

**Staff.** Anyone can use the approved templates. Reshare the file as it is.

"}, {"ref": "source_245", "relative_path": "brand/templates/email-templates.md", "heading_path": ["Email templates", "Retired"], "start_line": 310, "end_line": 312, "content": "## Retired

The "abandoned demo form" reminder went away in January 2026 because it felt like surveillance. The "We miss you" re-engagement email is also gone, and the replacement is one plain note asking whether to keep sending, with a single "Stay subscribed" button.

Rule coverage is Tesserline's real advantage. Its library is large, and it is well maintained. A security team that writes detection for a living, and wants to tune specific rules against specific techniques, will find more to work with there than in Quenchline. Compliance-driven teams that need to map detections to a control catalog may also find that the library saves work.

If you already run an incident response platform with a staffed queue around the clock, a detection-only product also fits neatly. Alerts flow to the people and playbooks you already have, and adding containment from a second vendor could mean two systems taking action on one incident.

Wickhold Quenchline takes a containment action only in contain mode. In observe mode it records what it would have done. Copy describing automatic containment must therefore be true of contain mode and should say so where a reader could assume otherwise. Containment actions are isolating a pod's network, freezing a process and draining a node. Do not add to the list without product confirmation.

Wickhold Evenburn reports drift, exposure paths and a fix order. It does not change a customer's environment by itself, and copy should not imply that it does.

"}, {"ref": "source_10", "relative_path": "brand/archive/blog/comparison-quenchline-vs-tesserline-2026.md", "heading_path": ["Comparison: Wickhold Quenchline and Tesserline for runtime containment", "How to decide"], "start_line": 52, "end_line": 66, "content": "## How to decide

Three questions will settle this for most teams.

1. **Who acts at 3am?** If a staffed team with its own tools does, detection-only may be enough. If the answer is one tired platform engineer, you want the tool to act.
2. **Who tunes detection?** If you have a detection engineer who enjoys this work, a big library helps. If nobody owns it, it will decay.
3. **What would you accept being automated?** If your organization will not let a tool isolate a production pod under any circumstances, Quenchline's main advantage is one you will not use. Better to know that before signing anything.

Some teams may reasonably run both, with Tesserline feeding a security operations queue and Quenchline holding the containment policy. We would ask anyone doing that to decide in advance which system is the source of record for an incident.

[Compare on your cluster](https://wickhold.example/trial)

*Tesserline is a trademark of its owner. This comparison reflects public information as of July 14, 2026 and will be reviewed when either product changes materially.*

*Wickhold is the runtime security company for teams that run Kubernetes. Its products contain failures early, so small fires stay small. Founded in 2019 and based in Denver, Wickhold serves more than 140 customers.*

Not everything in the illustration category qualifies here:

- **Hero illustrations only.** A spot illustration is transparent and square, and it sits inside body copy. Set as a hero, it leaves a small object floating in a wide band, so it is out.
- **No abstract backgrounds.** They have no focal point on their own, and a hero has no type set over it.
- **Tallow or Soot, matched to the post.** Illustration category rules allow either. For blog heroes, default to Tallow. Use Soot for incident retrospectives and long technical posts, so that the list page has some rhythm.

And from photography:

- **A person is allowed as the subject, but the post has to be about the work** and not a staff profile.

"}, {"ref": "source_15", "relative_path": "brand/voice/voice-and-tone-2026.md", "heading_path": ["Wickhold voice and tone", "Subjects that pull the voice off course"], "start_line": 191, "end_line": 208, "content": "## Subjects that pull the voice off course

Some topics drag writers back toward the register the rebrand left behind. These are the ones reviewers see most.

**AI agents.** Wickhold Leashgate, in early access, attracts the worst habits in the building, because the whole market is shouting about agents. Treat an agent as a workload with credentials and questionable judgment. Talk about tool calls, agent identity and the blast radius of an agent. Leave the future of work to other people. Anyone who has run production will recognize the problem from there, and that recognition is worth more than any amount of excitement.

**Compliance.** Dull on purpose. Certification status is a fact with one correct wording, and legal owns that wording. Copy the approved sentence and do not improve it. A nicer phrasing here is how a company ends up saying something untrue.

**Money.** Prices are stated flatly, with no "just", "only" or "starting from". Core is $18 per node per month. The reader can decide how they feel about that.

**Company news.** Funding, awards, headcount. Nobody is thrilled, excited or proud. The Series B was $46M in June 2024; that is a date and a number, and the sentence after it should say what changed for customers. If nothing changed for customers, ask whether the post needs to exist.

**Customers.** They did the work. Lowmoor Credit Union's on-call team runs its own incidents, and the product took one job off their list. Avoid "partnered with", "journey" and anything that casts us as the guide who showed them the way.

**Other approaches.** The voice doesn't sneer. Other kinds of product make real trade-offs, and a colleague would describe them as trade-offs: a heavier agent can see more and costs more on the node. Readers respect the writer who can state the other side accurately. Reviewers will cut anything that sounds like a playground.

**Open source.** Kubernetes, eBPF and Helm were here before us. We are users and we say so. Credit the projects, don't imply we invented the kernel feature, and don't describe a community as an "ecosystem we're proud to be part of".

The rebrand ran through a lot of ideas. Recording them saves the next person some time.

"}, {"ref": "source_23", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/00-visual-rules-common.md", "heading_path": ["Visual rules common to every image", "The image library and its metadata", "background"], "start_line": 98, "end_line": 107, "content": "### `background`

Three values.

- `transparent`: no ground at all. The image takes on whatever is behind it, which is why `safe_on` matters so much for these files.
- `solid`: a flat ground is part of the file, such as a logo on its panel or a hero illustration on Tallow.
- `scene`: the image has its own environment, as every photograph does. You never cut a scene out of its background, and we do not mask people or equipment out of photos.

A file marked `transparent` should be previewed on the actual ground before it ships. A bright fringe can look fine on one ground and show on another.

"}, {"ref": "source_24", "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md", "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "13. Updating published pieces"], "start_line": 211, "end_line": 216, "content": "## 13. Updating published pieces

"}, {"ref": "source_27", "relative_path": "brand/voice/voice-and-tone-2026.md", "heading_path": ["Wickhold voice and tone", "Tone by channel"], "start_line": 105, "end_line": 122, "content": "## Tone by channel

The voice stays the same. How much of it you get changes with the room.

**Landing pages.** The flattest we get. Mechanical, confident, short. The reader is deciding whether to spend ten more minutes, so tell them what the thing does on a cluster and let them go. "Wickhold Quenchline isolates the pod, freezes the process or drains the node, then writes down what it did."

**Blog.** The most room to think. Brand-voice posts walk through how something fails. Dov's posts can argue, and they should. A good post leaves the reader able to do one thing they could not do before, even if they never buy. Avoid the summary paragraph at the end. If the post worked, the reader was there.

**LinkedIn.** The company page is brand voice. Founder posts are where the personality lives. A post runs about 200 words, which suits one story and one point. Write as a person with a job, not a thought leader: no line breaks after every sentence, no "here's what I learned", no lists of lessons from an outage.

**X.** One fact, or one observation, in a dry tone. The account does not chase the news and does not reply to arguments about vendors. It's fine for a post to be plain. "The median time to contain a runtime incident is 7.4 hours [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report]. That is most of a night shift."

**Email.** One person writing to one person who is busy. Say why you are writing in the first sentence. Assume it is being read on a phone in a hallway. No "I hope this finds you well", and since these are brand emails, no "I" at all unless Maren signed it. Customer notices are the exception to everything else in this list and sound like the incident channel at the top of this document.

**Product UI and error text.** The closest thing we have to pure voice. What happened, what state things are in, what to do. "Containment action failed on node `ip-10-2-14-7`: agent unreachable. The pod is still running. Retry or drain the node." Chirpy empty states were tried in 2025 and came out after a customer saw one during a real incident.

**Case studies.** Third person, numbers up front, the customer's team as the subject of most sentences. Enough detail about their environment that a peer recognizes it. A case study that could describe any customer describes none of them.

"}, {"ref": "source_28", "relative_path": "brand/voice/voice-and-tone-2026.md", "heading_path": ["Wickhold voice and tone", "Start at 3am"], "start_line": 5, "end_line": 17, "content": "## Start at 3am

Anyone who writes for Wickhold should read an incident channel before writing a line of copy. Kofi Anselm's team keeps a few scrubbed transcripts for new hires. Skip the panic at the top of the thread and find the messages from whoever is running the incident. They tend to look like this:

> 03:14 UTC. A pod in `checkout` started a shell it has no reason to start.
> 03:14 UTC. Wickhold Quenchline froze the process and isolated the pod's network.
> 03:22 UTC. Rest of the namespace is quiet. Still unknown how the shell got there.
> Reading the image history now. Next update 03:45.

That is the voice. It says what happened, what is contained and what is next, in that order, and it stops. It has timestamps where other writers have adjectives. It admits the thing it does not know in the same flat tone as the thing it does. The person writing it is tired and is not going to make their tiredness your problem. Forty people are reading, half of them frightened, and the frightened ones calm down because of how the message is written.

Maren Tolliver and Dov Achterberg were on-call infrastructure leads before they founded this company in Denver in 2019. The voice is theirs by inheritance. The 2026 brand made it official: a wick is the one place a fire is allowed to exist. Production will catch fire in small ways, on ordinary nights, for dull reasons. The mission is to keep small failures from becoming big ones, and the copy should sound like it was written by people who consider that a normal day's work.

"}, {"ref": "source_33", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "4. Positioning", "Who it is for"], "start_line": 191, "end_line": 200, "content": "### Who it is for

Three groups share the buying decision. Their detailed profiles and the way to address each are kept in the persona documents. In brief:

"}, {"ref": "source_34", "relative_path": "brand/voice/voice-and-tone-2026.md", "heading_path": ["Wickhold voice and tone", "One fact, three rooms"], "start_line": 173, "end_line": 190, "content": "## One fact, three rooms

The same pair of numbers, set for three readers. The facts stay fixed and the weight moves.

On a landing page, where the reader is deciding whether to keep going:

> The median time to contain a runtime incident is 7.4 hours [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report]. Wickhold Quenchline contains a known-bad process in a median of 38 seconds in Wickhold lab benchmarks, 2026.

In a note to a CISO, where the number has to fit a conversation about risk:

> The median time to contain a runtime incident is 7.4 hours [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report]. Your team's own figure is the one to bring to the risk committee.

In a post for platform engineers, where the first response to a lab figure is suspicion:

> Wickhold Quenchline contains a known-bad process in a median of 38 seconds in Wickhold lab benchmarks, 2026. Your cluster is not our lab. Run it in observe mode and read what it would have done.

"}, {"ref": "source_35", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/00-visual-rules-common.md", "heading_path": ["Visual rules common to every image", "The image library and its metadata", "safe_on"], "start_line": 108, "end_line": 117, "content": "### `safe_on`

Three values, each describing the ground the image is designed to sit on.

- `light`: Tallow and other pale grounds only.
- `dark`: Soot and other deep grounds only.
- `any`: holds up on both.

Treat `safe_on` as a limit, the same way you treat `restrictions`. A `light` image on a dark layout is a defect even if you can still more or less see it. The layout's ground is what matters: a dark band halfway down a light page is a dark ground. When an image sits on a photo, or on Ember or Whetstone, neither word applies directly. "}, {"ref": "source_37", "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md", "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "8. Technical writing in marketing copy", "Terms we set one way"], "start_line": 154, "end_line": 177, "content": "### Terms we set one way

| Write | Not |
|---|---|
| Kubernetes | K8s, kube (fine in Slack, not in copy) |
| eBPF | EBPF, ebpf, e-BPF |
| containerd | Containerd, ContainerD |
| Helm, Helm chart | helm chart |
| pod, node, cluster, namespace | Pod, Node, Cluster, Namespace (unless it's the literal field or kind in code) |
| runtime (one word, all uses) | run-time, run time |
| on-call (adjective, plus the noun in our value "the next on-call"), on call (otherwise) | oncall |
| open source (noun), open-source (adjective) | opensource |
| cloud-native (adjective) | cloud native |
| tool call (noun), tool-call policy (adjective) | toolcall |
| AI agent | agentic AI, "AI worker", "digital employee" |
| CVE (uppercase, spell the ID in full: CVE-YYYY-NNNNN) | Cve, "a CVE" as a synonym for "an exploit" |
| CIS Benchmarks | CIS benchmarks |
| SOC 2 Type II (space, Roman numerals) | SOC2, SOC 2 Type 2 |
| PCI DSS | PCI-DSS |

Spell out an abbreviation on first use only if the reader might not know it. Platform engineers know what a CVE is. Board-level readers may need "time to contain" rather than an acronym we made up, and we don't use MTTC anywhere, because we'd then have to explain it.

**Security language.** Allowlist and denylist, not whitelist and blacklist. Primary and replica, not master and slave. If Kubernetes itself retains an old term in a literal field name, leave the field as it is.

- **At most seven words of overlay text**

The seven-word cap narrows what the social graphics rules allow. A stat card on any other surface can carry a measure line and a source. On LinkedIn it gets the number and the short label only.

| Overlay | Words | Verdict |
|---|---|---|

| Median time to contain: 7.4 hours | 6 | Good, source in the post |
| 11 minutes, down from 4 hours | 6 | Good, with Lowmoor named in the post |

Bullets are for parallel things. If a list reads like an argument, it's a paragraph.

**Citations give the source name, the year and the link, in brackets, right after the claim.**

The shape, exactly:

```text
41% of platform teams need more than six hours to contain a runtime incident [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report].
```

- Source name in full, as the source spells it.
- Comma, year. Comma, link. The full stop for the sentence goes outside the bracket.
- Link goes to the report or page itself, not a press release about it and not a search result. In a PDF or on a slide print the link out, because hyperlinks do not survive a screenshot.
- Use the same form everywhere, including LinkedIn and X. Yes, it's long on X. Plan the post around it.
- Two sources for one claim: two brackets. Do not merge them.
- A source we did not produce gets its own name in the bracket, even when a Wickhold page quotes it. Cite the original.
- In long pieces (report summaries, the blog), mention the survey base once near the first figure: "a survey of 412 platform and security leaders".

We tried numbered footnotes on the blog through most of 2025 and dropped them. The claim got quoted on LinkedIn, the footnote stayed behind, and the number went around with no source. A bracket travels with the sentence.

Customer results don't take a bracket when the customer is named in the sentence and the case study is linked from the page. Naming them is the source.

The record is here so that nobody spends a month rediscovering it.

"}, {"ref": "source_52", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "8. Typography", "Using them well"], "start_line": 352, "end_line": 363, "content": "### Using them well

Bricolage Grotesque is a display face. Below about 20 px its quirks turn into noise, so it should not be used for body text, buttons or table cells. Limit a page to the two headline weights in the table.

Plex Sans carries nearly everything else. Keep line lengths between 60 and 80 characters. On long pages a wider column is the first thing to go wrong.

Plex Mono has a job beyond code. Commands, flags, file names, YAML keys and other literal strings are set in mono inside body text, so a reader can see what to type. Node counts and timings in a table can also use it, because the digits line up. Do not use it for decoration or to make something feel technical. Engineers notice.

Email is the known exception. Mail clients ignore most web fonts, so the email stack falls back to a system sans-serif, and headlines in an email rely on weight and spacing to do the work.

Italic is for titles of reports and for the occasional stress. All caps are limited to small labels in a layout, and never to whole sentences.

"}, {"ref": "source_53", "relative_path": "brand/channels/blog-playbook.md", "heading_path": ["Writing for the Wickhold blog", "3. Post types"], "start_line": 37, "end_line": 48, "content": "## 3. Post types

**Engineering posts.** Written by Dov, Kofi or an engineer with an editor attached. How the eBPF agent attaches, what we learned from a kernel upgrade, why a containment action took longer than it should have. These carry the blog.

**How-to posts.** A task, steps, and what it looks like when it goes wrong: rolling out contain mode, reading an exposure path, writing a first tool-call policy for Leashgate in early access.

**Report posts.** One finding from the Containment Report, argued properly. We get four or five out of each report. Do not summarize the whole report in one post. That's what the report page does.

**Customer posts.** Built from a published case study, with the customer's own words where we have approval. These need Priit's sign-off every time, even when the numbers are already public.

**Founder posts.** Maren, on company decisions and what she learned from them. They're rare and marketing does not ghostwrite them. An editor can tidy.

"}, {"ref": "source_54", "relative_path": "brand/voice/voice-and-tone-2026.md", "heading_path": ["Wickhold voice and tone", "How the sentences go"], "start_line": 209, "end_line": 222, "content": "## How the sentences go

**Short first.** Most sentences run under twenty words. The long ones earn it by carrying a real sequence of events.

**Verbs do the work.** Name who did what. "Quenchline froze the process" over "the process was frozen". Past tense for incidents, present tense for what the product does.

**End early.** Our most common edit is deleting the last line of a paragraph. Writers tend to add one that restates the point in a nicer rhythm. Readers don't need it. This goes double for the final line of a piece.

**Ration the fire.** The tagline is "Small fires stay small." It carries the metaphor so the copy doesn't have to. A piece gets at most one fire image, and many pieces should have none. Nothing ignites, sparks, blazes or fans the flames. Slow Burn Summit gets to keep its name.

**Plain words for plain things.** "Use", "start", "stop", "run". Reach for the fancier word and the reader assumes something is being hidden.

**Don't argue with the reader's experience.** Telling a platform engineer that alerts are overwhelming is telling them what they had for breakfast. Start from what they know and add something.

"}, {"ref": "source_55", "relative_path": "brand/channels/linkedin-playbook.md", "heading_path": ["LinkedIn playbook", "Examples"], "start_line": 83, "end_line": 90, "content": "Nothing happened in that post. No product, no date, no number, and a reader who stops at the cut has learned only that we are thrilled.

Bad, the post with too many jobs:

> Our report is out, we're hiring in Denver, Slow Burn Summit registration is open, and Wickhold Evenburn has a new fix order view. Links in the comments.

That is four posts. Pick the one with a deadline.

"}, {"ref": "source_56", "relative_path": "brand/voice/voice-and-tone-2026.md", "heading_path": ["Wickhold voice and tone", "Tone by audience"], "start_line": 137, "end_line": 158, "content": "## Tone by audience

Humor depends on the audience, see each persona.

The personas hold the working rules for each reader, including what goes first. What follows is only the register, meaning how the voice sounds once you have chosen your content.

**CISOs.** Level and measured. Assume the reader will forward your paragraph to an audit committee without editing it, and write something they can forward. Risk, time and board language are their native terms: exposure, time to contain, residual risk, ownership. Short sentences, complete ones, no shorthand. Every sentence should survive being read aloud in a room that includes a lawyer.

**Platform engineers.** A good pull-request comment from a colleague you respect. Exact, brief, assumes competence, and shows its working. If there is a YAML snippet that makes the point, the prose can get out of its way. Marketing English reads as noise here and the page will be closed.

**DevSecOps.** These readers sit between the review queue and the pipeline, and they spend their days being the person who says no. Write to someone who is outnumbered: practical, on their side, and specific about what lands in their queue and what stays out of it.

**Compliance leads.** Careful nouns. This reader will notice the difference between "supports" and "meets", and will quote you. Their persona is still being written, so if the piece is aimed mainly at them, ask Noor before guessing.

**Customers mid-incident.** Pure 3am voice. Nothing about the product, nothing about the relationship, no reassurance that isn't backed by a fact. What we see, what we've done, when the next update comes.

**Finance and procurement.** They read a small part of what we write and they read it closely. Plain sentences, the price in the standard form, the terms where they expect them. Anything that sounds like enthusiasm reads to them as a negotiating position.

**Journalists.** Assume no interest in the product and real interest in what is happening to teams. Offer the finding, the method and a person to talk to. Don't send them a story with a hook in it; they have their own.

**Candidates and the community.** Warmer, plainer, and allowed to mention that the work is interesting. The same no-drama rules hold. Nobody here is a rockstar.

"}, {"ref": "source_57", "relative_path": "brand/voice/voice-and-tone-2026.md", "heading_path": ["Wickhold voice and tone", "What Wickhold believes"], "start_line": 37, "end_line": 40, "content": "## What Wickhold believes

"}, {"ref": "source_58", "relative_path": "brand/legal/approved-claims-2026.md", "heading_path": ["Approved claims, 2026", "6. Breach and incident references"], "start_line": 127, "end_line": 150, "content": "## 6. Breach and incident references

This section sets how Wickhold may talk about breaches and other public incidents, in any channel.

1. Never name a victim. That covers company names, product names, and descriptions that identify one ("a large regional retailer in the week it made the news").
2. No humor. Not in the copy, not in the image, not in a speaker's aside.
3. Nothing within 30 days of a public incident. Count from the first public disclosure. For the 30 days, Wickhold does not publish, post, send or sponsor anything that refers to the incident or that is plainly timed to it. An incident is not a marketing hook.

After 30 days, a breach may be discussed in general terms only, as a pattern and without identifying anyone. A technical analysis of a technique is fine if it does not rely on the incident for attention.

The rules cover paid media, social, email, blog posts, sales sequences, talks and replies to journalists. They apply to personal LinkedIn accounts when the post mentions Wickhold or its products. Press inquiries about a live incident go to Ilse Varga-Holm, and nobody comments before she has spoken to me.

If a campaign in market could be read as a reaction to a new public incident, whoever notices it pauses it and tells Ilse. Nobody will be criticized for pausing. Sales may answer a direct customer question about an incident with facts about the customer's own deployment. It may not use the question as an opening.

Incidents at Wickhold customers are never discussed without the customer's written approval, whatever their age. The approved Lowmoor material is the model. It has a figure and no drama.

Not approved:

> After last week's breach at a regional bank, can your team afford another six hours?

Approved, more than 30 days after any related event:

> When a pod misbehaves, Wickhold Quenchline in contain mode can isolate its network while the on-call engineer works out what happened.

"}, {"ref": "source_59", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "2. Mission"], "start_line": 61, "end_line": 82, "content": "## 2. Mission

**Keep small failures from becoming big ones.**

The mission is written for the people who run production. A failed deployment, a process that should not be running, a credential in the wrong place: these happen every week in any serious cluster, and they stay dull when somebody contains them early. The company exists to keep them dull.

Three things follow from that wording, and they are the reasons it was chosen.

It accepts that failures happen. A company that claims failures will not happen has stopped talking to engineers. Founders Maren and Dov spent years as on-call infrastructure leads before starting Wickhold in Denver in March 2019, and neither of them has ever met a system that did not fail.

It measures success by size. A contained incident still gets logged, reviewed and fixed. The win is that it stayed at one pod and did not reach the node, or stayed at one node and did not reach the cluster.

It says "keep", which is ongoing work. Containment is something a team does with good tools, every week. The mission gives the product a role in that work and leaves the credit for the outcome with the customer's on-call team.

Use the mission on recruiting pages, in all-hands decks and in the opening of long-form pieces about the company. It is an internal compass first. It should not be pasted on product pages as a slogan, because the tagline already does that job.

A few sentences show the difference between using the mission and hanging it on the wall.

Good, from a recruiting page: "We build software that keeps small failures from becoming big ones. If you have been paged at 3am, you already know why that matters."

Weak: "Our mission is to revolutionize the way the world thinks about failure." It's bigger than the company, and it says nothing an on-call engineer would recognize.

Sales, this is the sheet to use before you answer a security questionnaire. If a deck or an old email says something different, the deck or the email is out of date.

| Program | Status | What you may say |
|---|---|---|
| SOC 2 Type II | Held. Renewed January 2026 | "Wickhold holds SOC 2 Type II." |

**FedRAMP.** Never claim FedRAMP authorization or certification. The approved wording above is the only wording. It goes in copy exactly as written, including the word "pursuing".

These are banned in every channel, spoken or written: "FedRAMP Authorized", "FedRAMP certified", "FedRAMP Ready", "FedRAMP compliant", "FedRAMP equivalent", "built to FedRAMP standards". Agency buyers read those words literally, and a false statement to a federal buyer is a contract and legal problem, whatever the deal size.

The status changes when authorization is complete and published, and this sheet says so. An assessor's visit, a sponsor conversation, or a positive meeting does not change it. Do not give prospects a target date. We do not publish one. If a federal prospect presses, the answer is the sentence above and an offer to connect them with me.

Good, in an answer to a questionnaire:

> Wickhold holds SOC 2 Type II, renewed January 2026. Wickhold is pursuing FedRAMP Moderate authorization. We can share the SOC 2 report under NDA.

Bad:

> We're basically FedRAMP Authorized, the paperwork is just finishing up.

**SOC 2.** The report goes out under NDA through the account team, never by public link. Say "Type II" every time. Say "held" or "renewed", and do not say "SOC 2 certified", because SOC 2 ends in an attestation report and not a certificate.

**Questionnaires and RFPs.** Security questionnaires go through the account team, and any answer about certifications is copied from this sheet. If a form offers only "Yes" or "No" for FedRAMP, answer "No", and use the comments box for the approved sentence. Do not tick a box in the hope of explaining later.

"}, {"ref": "source_63", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "10. Accessibility summary"], "start_line": 434, "end_line": 450, "content": "## 10. Accessibility summary

Accessible work is part of the brand standard, and it is checked at review alongside everything else. The reasoning is simple enough: engineers read documentation on bad monitors, on phones and at 3am, and some of them have low vision or are color-blind. Work that only functions in perfect conditions fails the people it is meant for.

In summary, four commitments apply across all marketing work:

- Text is readable against its background. The palette has been measured, and not every pairing is suitable for small text. Ember in particular needs care.
- Images carry a text description, so nobody loses the point of a piece because an image did not load or cannot be seen.
- Meaning is never carried by color alone. A chart or status needs a label, a shape or a pattern too.
- Pages work with a keyboard and at high zoom, and video has captions.

The misses that come up most at review are predictable. A chart legend that relies on Ember versus Verdigris alone is hard to read for some color-blind readers, since those two are close in lightness. An Ember link in a paragraph looks fine on a designer's monitor and is hard to read on a laptop in daylight. Text set into an image can't be read by a screen reader and can't be translated. Video exported from a webinar tool often ships with captions switched off.

Accessibility review belongs to whoever does the brand check on a piece, and it isn't a separate stage. If a template fails, Noor's team fixes the template, so the same miss doesn't come back in every piece made from it.

The specific requirements are in the visual accessibility guidance, and the measured color pairs are in the logo and color addendum. Bricolage Grotesque's limit on small sizes, in section 8, is as much an accessibility point as a matter of taste.

"}, {"ref": "source_73", "relative_path": "brand/channels/blog-playbook.md", "heading_path": ["Writing for the Wickhold blog", "8. Working with engineers who don't want to write"], "start_line": 105, "end_line": 117, "content": "## 8. Working with engineers who don't want to write

Most of our best material is in the heads of people who would rather fix a kernel bug. Don't send them a blank doc. Book 30 minutes, ask them to walk you through the last hard thing they fixed, and record it with their permission. Write the draft from the recording and send it back for correction. An engineer who won't write 1,000 words will happily rewrite the 200 you got wrong.

Keep their phrasing where you can. If someone says the agent "falls over politely" on a read-only kernel, that goes in. Their name goes on the post, and they read the final version before it goes live. If they ask to take something out, take it out, and don't argue about it in the review thread.

Questions that tend to produce a post:

- What did you assume about this before you got paged?
- What's the command you wish you had run first?
- What does the failure look like from the outside?
- What did you change afterward, and did it hold?

"}, {"ref": "source_78", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "6. Logo summary"], "start_line": 272, "end_line": 283, "content": "## 6. Logo summary

The mark is a geometric W whose center stroke rises as a wick, tipped by one Ember dot. It says the same thing as the brand idea: a straight, deliberate structure with one small, controlled point of heat at the top. The dot is the only warm thing in the mark, and that is the reason to protect it. Used alongside the wordmark "Wickhold", it forms the lockup, which is the default in most layouts.

There are four approved variants: ink on transparent, reversed on transparent, on a Tallow panel, and on a Soot panel. Exact file specifications, clear space and minimum sizes are in the logo and color addendum. How to choose among the variants for a given layout belongs to the logo-in-context guidance.

The 2024 shield-and-flame logo is retired. It still appears in the archive and in a few old files, and it should not be used in anything new.

The logo appears once in a layout, and it usually doesn't need to be large. Confidence in a mark shows in how much room it's given, so a modest logo with space around it is better than a big one crowded by other elements. In the product, the mark appears in the console header and on the sign-in page. Screens that a customer works in all day don't need it anywhere else.

Two pieces of history are worth keeping in mind. In the first month after launch, the product team shipped a loading state with a flickering dot, and customers read it as an error. It was withdrawn. The dot does not move. And early on, several people tried turning the W into a pattern for backgrounds and swag. The mark loses its meaning when it repeats, because the whole point is that there is one of it. Use it once per layout.

"}, {"ref": "source_84", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "4. Positioning", "How the position developed"], "start_line": 183, "end_line": 190, "content": "### How the position developed

The company did not change what it builds. Quenchline has offered detection and containment since September 2020. What changed is which half of that sentence the brand leads with. In the 2024 identity, the watching came first and containment was a feature. In the 2026 identity, containment is the point and detection is what makes it possible. Detection still matters to buyers and should be described accurately. It just isn't the headline.

Evenburn fits the same logic from the other direction. Posture work reduces how much there is to catch fire, and it gives the team a fix order so that the worst exposure path gets closed first. The story to tell is about keeping the fuel down, and it shouldn't be told as a second, separate product category.

Leashgate extends the idea to AI agents, which now take actions inside customers' environments. An agent with broad tools is a new kind of workload that can make a mistake quickly. Leashgate sets out what that agent may do and keeps a record of what it did. It is in early access, and the position should be described with that in mind: a direction the company is working in, with real customers trying it.

"}, {"ref": "source_85", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "8. Typography", "Slides and documents"], "start_line": 364, "end_line": 369, "content": "### Slides and documents

Slide titles use Bricolage Grotesque at 40 pt or larger, and body text in Plex Sans never goes below 18 pt. The master deck template and the document templates have all of this built in, so start there. Fonts should come from the shared font folder, because a copy downloaded from elsewhere can be a different version and shift the line breaks in someone else's slides.

A piece of long-form writing, such as a report, can use Plex Sans for captions and pull quotes. Pull quotes stay in Plex Sans and are not an excuse for a third display style.

"}, {"ref": "source_86", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "5. Brand architecture", "Reports and events"], "start_line": 251, "end_line": 258, "content": "### Reports and events

- **Slow Burn Summit.** Wickhold's own customer conference, in Denver each September. The 2026 edition ran September 15 to 16. The event may have its own title treatment, set in the brand type, and it uses the Wickhold logo.
- **Field Day.** Small regional customer meetups. Field Days use a shared template and do not get individual branding.

Webinars, workshops and one-off programs are described in plain words and do not get a brand of their own. A proposal for a podcast with its own name and cover art was turned down last year for this reason. A topic that needs its own identity to be interesting probably isn't interesting.

"}, {"ref": "source_87", "relative_path": "brand/voice/voice-and-tone-2026.md", "heading_path": ["Wickhold voice and tone", "What Wickhold believes", "Admit limits"], "start_line": 77, "end_line": 80, "content": "### Admit limits

One of the company values, and the one marketing finds hardest. Every product we sell has an edge. Wickhold Evenburn finds drift and exposure paths; it does not contain anything. Quenchline contains what is running; it does not patch the image it came from. Saying so costs a little in the moment and buys a lot of belief for the next claim on the page. Engineers look for the catch. When they find we already named it, they keep reading.

"}, {"ref": "source_88", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/accessibility.md", "heading_path": ["Image accessibility", "Contrast: 4.5:1 for text"], "start_line": 25, "end_line": 47, "content": "## Contrast: 4.5:1 for text

Text on any image or graphic meets at least 4.5:1 against what is directly behind it. We apply the same floor to all sizes, including large headlines. A designer will point out that the web standard relaxes for large type. We know. The single number is easier to check, and a stat card shrinks to thumbnail size in a feed, where large type stops being large. This floor governs images. Layouts follow the logo and color addendum.

Measured ratios for the palette:

| Pair | Ratio | Text allowed? |
|---|---|---|
| Soot on Tallow | 15.5:1 | Yes |

We will have our own bad days: a bad agent release, a late fix, a false containment that drained a node it should have left alone. The values cover this before anything else does. Say what happened. Contain first. Admit limits. Leave it better for the next on-call.

In practice:

- Lead with what happened to the customer's systems, in their terms.
- Use "we" and an active verb. "We shipped a policy update that drained nodes it should not have." "An issue occurred" is not a sentence we publish.
- Apologize once, plainly, in one short sentence. Then get on with the facts.
- Say what is still unknown.
- Say when the next update comes, and hit that time even if there's nothing new.

Dov signs off anything technical. Priit Salonen reads anything that touches a contract. Nobody in marketing edits the facts for tone.

"}, {"ref": "source_93", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "9. Photography and illustration direction", "Photography"], "start_line": 389, "end_line": 394, "content": "### Photography

Photographs show real work in real places: available light, working rooms and real infrastructure, warm and slightly underexposed. The feeling to aim for is the quiet of a team that has things under control, late in the day, with the lights half on. People are shown doing what they actually do. The 2024 look of bright, staged collaboration has gone, as has its blue tint.

A useful test is to ask whether an on-call engineer would recognize the room. A cable tray with a handwritten label passes. A spotless corridor of lights does not.

"}, {"ref": "source_94", "relative_path": "brand/voice/word-list.md", "heading_path": ["Word list", "Banned terms"], "start_line": 5, "end_line": 26, "content": "## Banned terms

There are thirteen. They stay out of headlines, body copy, decks, alt text and speaker notes that leave the building. When one shows up in a draft it usually marks the spot where the writer ran out of facts, so deleting it rarely fixes the sentence. Find the fact.

| Term | Why it is out | What to do instead |
|---|---|---|
| seamless | Putting an eBPF agent on every node has seams: a kernel check, a Helm upgrade, a stretch in observe mode. Platform engineers know this and stop reading when told otherwise. | Say what the rollout takes. |
| robust | Strong against what? The word claims a result and skips the test. | Name the failure the thing survived. |
| leverage | A finance word doing a job that "use" does for free. | Use "use". |
| best-in-class | No class, no judge, no source. It cannot pass "say the number, then stop". | Give the figure and where it came from. |
| next-gen | Every product in this market has been next-gen at some point. The word ages the day it ships. | Say what it does on a node today. |
| single pane of glass | Our readers have been sold this pane many times and own several. It also describes watching, and the job here is containing. | Name the screen and what it shows. |
| holistic | Usually covering for a gap. If something spans cloud and cluster, those two words are shorter and checkable. | List what is covered. |
| unlock | Implies the customer's own work was locked up and we hold the key. Drags padlocks into the room as well. | Say what the reader can now do. |
| empower | The readers already have root. Nobody here hands out power. | Say what changed for them, in a verb they would use. |
| cutting-edge | A claim about us, and an undated one. eBPF is well past being new, and that is one reason it is safe to run in production. | Name the technique. |
| game-changing | An incident is nobody's game, and the claim has no number attached. | Give the before and after. |
| prevent all | A promise no security product can keep. Includes "prevents all", which is the same promise with better grammar. | See the verbs below. |
| stop all | Same promise, same problem. A CISO who reads this line once will discount the rest of the page. | See the verbs below. |

The prose test: if a sentence still reads as true after you swap the product for a toaster, it needed a fact and got an adjective.

"}, {"ref": "source_95", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "3. Values"], "start_line": 83, "end_line": 108, "content": "## 3. Values

There are four, and they are written the way an on-call lead would say them.

**Say what happened.**
Report the event in plain order: what occurred, what was affected, what was done, what is next. This applies to incident reports, release notes, customer emails and the company's own mistakes. When a release goes badly, the customer note says so in the first sentence.

Good: "The last Wickhold Quenchline release raised CPU use on nodes running older kernels. A fix shipped on Tuesday. Here is how to check whether you were affected."

Bad: "We're always working to improve performance, and our latest update includes important enhancements."

**Contain first.**
In an incident, limit the damage before explaining it. In marketing, the same ordering applies: the first thing a reader gets is the thing that helps them, and the story of how it came about can wait. The value also sets the company's posture. Wickhold talks about containing, limiting and slowing. A promise of a world with no incidents is a promise no honest vendor can keep.

Good: "At Lowmoor Credit Union, time to contain fell from 4 hours to 11 minutes across 220 nodes."

That example gives the result with no adjectives around it and leaves the reader to decide what it means.

**Admit limits.**
Every product has edges, and engineers find them within a week. Naming a limit in advance costs less than having a customer discover it during a bad night, and it makes everything else the company says easier to believe.

Good: "Wickhold Quenchline works at runtime. It does not review code before it ships."

**Leave it better for the next on-call.**
This one comes straight from the founders. When an on-call shift ends, the next person should find the runbook updated, the noisy alert tuned and the handoff note written. Inside marketing it means naming source files sensibly, recording why a decision was made, and putting a correction in the document that was wrong and not only in a thread. It is why the "tried and dropped" list in section 1 exists.

"}, {"ref": "source_96", "relative_path": "brand/voice/word-list.md", "heading_path": ["Word list", "Preferred terms"], "start_line": 27, "end_line": 38, "content": "## Preferred terms

**Workload, not asset.** Customers run workloads, and that is the word they use in their own runbooks. "Asset" comes from inventory spreadsheets and suggests a thing that sits still. A workload moves, restarts and misbehaves, which is why it needs a runtime product. Inside the marketing team "asset" still means a blog post or an image file; that use never reaches a customer.

**Contain, limit and slow, rather than prevent.** This is the company's argument in three verbs. Something will go wrong on a Tuesday night regardless of what anyone buys. Wickhold Quenchline contains what is already running. Wickhold Evenburn limits exposure. Wickhold Leashgate limits what an agent can reach. "Slow" is the honest verb when the action buys time and does not end the problem. Also keep "eliminate" and "eradicate" out of it; they are "prevent" in a bigger coat.

Use "contain" only when a containment action actually happens. Detection on its own is detection.

One exception came out of a release-notes review. A line saying a patch prevents a crash in the agent is describing our own bug, so it can stay. The rule covers promises about what happens to customers, and a changelog entry makes none.

**Customers, not clients.** Clients have an account manager and a lunch. Customers run our agent in production and page us. A "client" in the software sense stays: `kubectl` is a client, an email client is a client. "Users" is fine when you mean the people logged in to the console, because a customer is the whole company.

"}, {"ref": "source_97", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "11. Governance", "Order of authority"], "start_line": 455, "end_line": 467, "content": "### Order of authority

When two sources conflict, the higher one on this list wins:

1. **Legal-approved claims.** The approved claims, certification status, regional rules and customer quote policy owned by Priit Salonen, General Counsel.
2. **These 2026 guidelines**, together with the logo and color addendum, which has the same standing.
3. **Channel playbooks.** The working guides for each channel.
4. **Everything else.** This includes the voice and style documents, messaging, personas, product overviews, templates, sales material, meeting notes and Slack.

So the order is: legal-approved claims, then the 2026 guidelines, then channel playbooks, then everything else.

A lower source is not void. It applies wherever nothing above it speaks to the question. A template's rule, or a decision recorded in meeting notes or Slack by the person who owns the topic, is followed like any other rule until a higher source contradicts it. The order settles conflicts and does not rank importance. If a document at the bottom of the list has the only rule on a subject, that is the rule.

"}, {"ref": "source_98", "relative_path": "brand/voice/voice-and-tone-2026.md", "heading_path": ["Wickhold voice and tone", "Founder voice and brand voice"], "start_line": 85, "end_line": 104, "content": "## Founder voice and brand voice

There are two voices at Wickhold, and they have one hard line between them.

**Founder voice is first person singular, and it is signed.** Maren writes as "I". Her posts carry her name. She gets to have feelings and doubts, tell a story from a bad night in 2017, and be wrong in public. Dov's technical posts work the same way and are signed "Dov".

**Brand voice never says "I" or "we think".** Website, product pages, company LinkedIn, the company X account, email, decks, reports: no first person singular, ever. "We believe", "we feel" and "in our view" are "we think" in different shoes, and they go too.

**Brand voice uses "Wickhold" or "we" for facts only.** Things that happened, things that are true of the company, things a lawyer could check.

| Fine in brand voice | Not in brand voice |
|---|---|
| We renewed SOC 2 Type II in January 2026. | We think SOC 2 matters. |
| Wickhold serves more than 140 customers. | I've talked to a lot of platform teams. |
| Containment is where incidents are won or lost. | We believe containment is where incidents are won or lost. |

The third row is the useful one. Brand voice still holds opinions. It states them as flat sentences, the way the on-call lead does, and lets the reader disagree. "We think" adds nothing except a hedge.

Practicalities. Nobody else writes as "I" in Wickhold content. Kofi's developer posts and anything from the wider team run in brand voice under a byline, because a byline is credit and a founder post is a person speaking for themselves. Customer quotes are quotes and say whatever was approved. If the content team drafts for Maren, she reads it and changes it before her name goes on, and a post that she has not read does not go out. In the spring a joint Maren-and-Dov byline was tried on one post; "I" became unreadable after two paragraphs, so that was dropped. One author per post.

"}, {"ref": "source_101", "relative_path": "brand/archive/blog/comparison-quenchline-vs-tesserline-2026.md", "heading_path": ["Comparison: Wickhold Quenchline and Tesserline for runtime containment", "What Quenchline does not do"], "start_line": 46, "end_line": 51, "content": "## What Quenchline does not do

Quenchline does not cover workloads outside Kubernetes. If a large share of your estate is on plain virtual machines, its coverage will stop at the cluster edge, and a broader detection product may suit you better. Quenchline also ships with fewer rules than Tesserline, so a team that wants fine-grained, hand-tuned detection on specific techniques will find it less flexible.

Automated containment also carries a risk that detection-only products do not have. A badly written policy can isolate a healthy pod. We recommend rolling out contain mode a policy at a time for exactly that reason.

"}, {"ref": "source_102", "relative_path": "brand/channels/blog-playbook.md", "heading_path": ["Writing for the Wickhold blog", "4. Shape of a post"], "start_line": 49, "end_line": 68, "content": "## 4. Shape of a post

A title that says what the reader will get. Then the intro. Then three to five sections with descriptive headings. Then an ending that tells the reader what to do on Monday.

Titles we liked:

- Contain mode, one namespace at a time
- What drift looks like after a Helm upgrade
- The six hours after detection
- Writing your first tool-call policy for Wickhold Leashgate, in early access

Titles we rewrote:

- "5 Kubernetes Security Mistakes You're Making Right Now" became "Five findings we see in most new clusters"
- "Everything You Need To Know About eBPF" became "What our eBPF agent can and can't see"

Section headings should still make sense if they're all someone reads. "Background" and "The solution" tell the reader nothing.

End on the practical next step, then one call to action to the most relevant page. Don't summarize what you just said. If the post was good, they remember. Don't add a paragraph about Wickhold at the bottom either, as the footer handles that.

**No rhetorical question as the first line of any asset.** Blog post, landing page hero, email (subject line and first sentence both), LinkedIn post, X post, video script, slide one of a deck.

"Is your cluster ready for the next incident?" tells the reader nothing and asks them to do the writer's work. It's also the most common opening in our category, so it reads as noise. Open on a fact, an event or a claim.

| Don't open with | Open with |
|---|---|
| What would you do if a pod started a shell at 3am? | A pod in `checkout` started a shell at 03:14 UTC. |
| Tired of alert fatigue? | Most alerts at 3am are about something that already stopped mattering. |

Real questions later in a piece are fine. An FAQ section is full of them and that's what it is for, as long as the page opens on a statement.

"}, {"ref": "source_105", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "4. Positioning", "Testing a campaign idea"], "start_line": 162, "end_line": 172, "content": "### Testing a campaign idea

Before a concept goes to design, Ilse's team asks four questions of it.

1. Could any other security vendor run this with their logo on it? If so, it isn't the position.
2. Does it depend on the reader being scared? If so, drop it.
3. Does it show containment, or only talk about it?
4. Would the customer's on-call lead forward it to a colleague without a sarcastic comment?

The "Quiet night" concept from the 2026 launch passed all four, and it became the opening of the launch film: a dark office, one screen, a log line reading that a pod had been isolated, and an engineer who doesn't appear because she is asleep at home.

"}, {"ref": "source_106", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "4. Positioning", "Where the category goes wrong"], "start_line": 150, "end_line": 161, "content": "### Where the category goes wrong

Security marketing has habits that readers have learned to skip. The position is partly defined by not having them.

| Category habit | What Wickhold does |
|---|---|
| Opens with a frightening scenario | Opens with what a team can do about the problem |
| Promises total coverage | Says what is covered and names what is not |
| Sells the dashboard | Shows the containment action and its log entry |
| Treats the on-call engineer as a victim | Treats the on-call engineer as the expert |
| Uses a survey to alarm | Uses a survey to size a problem, then stops |

"}, {"ref": "source_107", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "7. Color", "What replaced Cobalt"], "start_line": 298, "end_line": 303, "content": "### What replaced Cobalt

Cobalt, the primary color from 2024, was retired on February 10, 2026, and **Ember `#C2501F` replaced it as the primary color**. Cobalt should not appear in any new work. Ember is not used the way Cobalt was. Cobalt covered whole slides, hero bands and booth walls. Ember is a small, deliberate point of heat, and a layout built around it should look mostly like Tallow or Soot.

The reasons for the change were practical as well as symbolic. The category is full of blue, and in side-by-side tests of competitor pages Wickhold's old pages were hard to pick out. A warm orange-brown also ties the color to the brand idea, since it is the color of a banked coal. It is deliberately neither a bright hazard orange nor an alarm red, because the brand is not trying to raise a reader's pulse.

"}, {"ref": "source_110", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/00-visual-rules-common.md", "heading_path": ["Visual rules common to every image", "Picking an image: the order"], "start_line": 122, "end_line": 131, "content": "## Picking an image: the order

1. Decide the category and read that page.
2. Decide the content type and read that page.
3. Search the library. Search by description and by a few different words, since tags are uneven.
4. Open the record. Read `restrictions` and `usage_rights` first, then `background`, `safe_on` and size.
5. Look at the picture itself at full size against the current identity. Metadata does not catch everything.
6. Check it against the rest of the layout, on the real ground.
7. Add it to the draft with its `id` noted in the review comment, so Brand can trace it.

"}, {"ref": "source_111", "relative_path": "brand/voice/voice-and-tone-2026.md", "heading_path": ["Wickhold voice and tone", "Tone by channel"], "start_line": 123, "end_line": 136, "content": "**The Containment Report.** Annual, every April, and the most formal thing we publish. It reads like a clinical note: findings in flat declaratives, method stated early, no pitch in the body. The product can appear at the end, briefly, once the reader has had what they came for.

**Release notes.** Past tense, specific, no selling. A bug we fixed is described as a bug.

**Press.** Third person, plain, one idea per release. The quote from Maren is the only place with any warmth, and she writes it herself.

**Sales decks and talk tracks.** Same facts, same claims, slightly warmer because a person is in the room. If a slide would embarrass the on-call lead, it comes out.

**Webinars and video.** Script it as speech, then cut a third. Two people talking through a real incident timeline beats one person reading slides. No stock intro music with a heartbeat in it, and no voiceover that sounds like a trailer.

**Support replies.** These are written by the support team and we don't police them, but the same habit applies: repeat what you saw, say what you did, say what happens next. A reply that begins by thanking the customer for their patience has already lost them.

**Events.** Slow Burn Summit in Denver is the one place where we are among friends, and it can sound like that. The stage voice is relaxed and first-name, and the facts on the slides are still the facts. Field Day is smaller and closer to a conversation in a car park. Booth copy is brand voice: short, mechanical, no shouting.
