Owner: Noor Eskelund, Head of Brand. Last edited September 2026, after the Slow Burn Summit push showed us how many people pick images without opening the metadata.

These rules apply to every image Wickhold publishes: a blog hero, a chart in a white paper, a slide a sales engineer drops into a customer call, a banner at a Field Day. If you are holding an image and wondering whether this page applies, it does.

", "document_id": "7393a98e-d420-4e3a-a620-f4bf13834b9d", "end_line": 6, "heading_path": ["Visual rules common to every image"], "relative_path": "brand/visuals/00-visual-rules-common.md", "start_line": 1}, {"chunk_id": "930be8e8-ae39-4b4c-92f1-fb0b444f55be", "content": "## How the visual rules are layered

Three layers, read in this order.

1. **This page.** Applies to everything.
2. **The category.** What kind of image is it? Photo, illustration, icon, logo, product screenshot, chart, social graphic, event graphic, legal and trust imagery, anything showing a person.
3. **The content type.** Where is it going? Blog hero, LinkedIn, X, email header, landing page.

Most images touch one rule from each layer, and some touch two categories. A photo of a staff member at a customer site is photography and consent at once, and it has to pass both.

A lower layer can narrow a higher one. The illustration category accepts several formats, for example, and the blog hero page accepts fewer of them. In that case follow the narrower rule for that placement, and the broader rule stays true everywhere else. A lower layer cannot loosen this page. If a content-type page seems to let you do something this page forbids, bring it to Brand, because one of the two pages is wrong and we want to fix it.

Per-campaign exceptions go through Noor's exception log. Without an entry there, if a campaign needs something new, the rule changes for everybody or the campaign changes.

", "document_id": "7393a98e-d420-4e3a-a620-f4bf13834b9d", "end_line": 20, "heading_path": ["Visual rules common to every image", "How the visual rules are layered"], "relative_path": "brand/visuals/00-visual-rules-common.md", "start_line": 7}, {"chunk_id": "849c4a03-5ccb-4481-baf9-1a0a8bee9d61", "content": "## The two rules that come up every week

", "document_id": "7393a98e-d420-4e3a-a620-f4bf13834b9d", "end_line": 22, "heading_path": ["Visual rules common to every image", "The two rules that come up every week"], "relative_path": "brand/visuals/00-visual-rules-common.md", "start_line": 21}, {"chunk_id": "dc3bc010-0485-41ce-88ec-cb162a2de295", "content": "### No generated text in any image

No image contains text produced by an image model or baked into artwork by a tool that does not treat it as live type. Models misspell product names, invent letterforms and produce near-English that survives one quick look and then gets screenshotted by a customer. We had a test hero in spring where a wall sign read almost like "Quenchline". Nobody caught it until it was in a review deck.

Text in a Wickhold image is set by a person, in the design tool, in the brand typefaces, as a separate layer over finished art. That covers overlays, labels, chart annotations and callouts.

Three things do not count as generated text:

- Words that are really in the scene: a printed rack label, a whiteboard someone wrote on, a door sign. Check that they say nothing embarrassing and name nobody outside the company.
- Real interface text in a true product screenshot.
- The wordmark, which is a vector file, placed by a person.

Some placements allow no overlay at all and others cap it. The content-type page has the number.

", "document_id": "7393a98e-d420-4e3a-a620-f4bf13834b9d", "end_line": 36, "heading_path": ["Visual rules common to every image", "The two rules that come up every week", "No generated text in any image"], "relative_path": "brand/visuals/00-visual-rules-common.md", "start_line": 23}, {"chunk_id": "c37df191-6216-45a0-a492-50686e14a2e5", "content": "### One focal point

Every image has one focal point. A reader should be able to say what the image is of after a second's look. If two things compete, crop or pick another image.

Tests we use in review:

- Squint at it. One shape or area should hold.
- Shrink it to a thumbnail. Something should still be identifiable.
- Describe it in one short sentence without "and". "An engineer reading a terminal in a dark room" passes. "A team at a table and a wall of monitors and a logo on the door" does not.

Collages, split screens and before-and-after pairs fail this unless they are charts, where the comparison is the single point.

", "document_id": "7393a98e-d420-4e3a-a620-f4bf13834b9d", "end_line": 48, "heading_path": ["Visual rules common to every image", "The two rules that come up every week", "One focal point"], "relative_path": "brand/visuals/00-visual-rules-common.md", "start_line": 37}, {"chunk_id": "974c9dd1-f990-47ba-bc47-a49f901d010c", "content": "## Other rules for all images

**Current identity only.** Ember `#C2501F`, Soot `#15181C`, Tallow `#F4EFE6`, with Whetstone `#5E6B73` and Verdigris `#2F8F83` as secondary colors. Bricolage Grotesque, IBM Plex Sans and IBM Plex Mono for any type on an image. Anything leaning on the 2024 blue palette or the 2024 logo is out, however good it looks. Some of those images are still in the library with no flag on them, so your eye is part of this check.

**No third-party marks.** No real product logos on laptop lids, no cloud provider marks on diagrams, no conference logos in a crop unless the agreement with that organizer allows it. Customer marks are a legal matter and go through Legal first.

**No watermarks,** no preview overlays, no leftover crop marks. If an image arrived with a watermark, its rights are not what you think they are.

**Do not stretch, tint or recolor library files.** Crop freely within the category's limits. Stretching breaks the proportions of the art and recoloring breaks the palette. Filters are out too: the warm look comes from the source image, and a filter laid on a cool image only makes it look cool and filtered. If an image needs a color change to fit, it is the wrong image.

**Export for the placement.** WebP or PNG for web, PNG where transparency matters, SVG for logos and icons when the placement accepts it. Keep web images under 400 KB unless the content-type page says otherwise. JPEG artifacts around Ember shapes are very visible, so check flat illustration at full size after compressing.

**Nothing that frightens.** Images follow the same stance as the copy. Show the small fire or the calm room, and skip the alarm. Red alert screens, countdown timers, sirens and skulls have no place here, even as a joke in an engineering post.

", "document_id": "7393a98e-d420-4e3a-a620-f4bf13834b9d", "end_line": 62, "heading_path": ["Visual rules common to every image", "Other rules for all images"], "relative_path": "brand/visuals/00-visual-rules-common.md", "start_line": 49}, {"chunk_id": "85f52c31-27b5-4fe5-921a-ea411fb55932", "content": "## The image library and its metadata

Every approved image lives in the image library, and every image in it has a metadata record. Do not pick from the thumbnail grid and stop there. The thumbnail does not show you the limits on the image.

| Field | What it tells you |
|---|---|
| `id`, `filename` | Identity. Filenames were set by different people across several years and tell you little. |
| `type`, `title` | Rough category and a human label. |
| `description` | What is in the picture. Often thin, sometimes empty. |
| `tags` | Search help. Inconsistent, so never treat a missing tag as meaning anything. |
| `usage_rights` | The grant we hold for the file. |
| `restrictions` | The limits on this particular image. See below. |
| `added_date` | When it entered the library, which is not when it was made. |
| `source`, `attribution` | Where it came from. In-house work reads `internal-production`, and `attribution` is usually empty or names the in-house team. Empty attribution means no credit line is needed. |
| `width`, `height` | Pixel size. Check before you plan a crop. |
| `background` | How the image relates to what sits behind it. See below. |
| `safe_on` | Which grounds it can sit on. See below. |
| `variant_of` | Points at the parent when the image is one version of another. |

", "document_id": "7393a98e-d420-4e3a-a620-f4bf13834b9d", "end_line": 81, "heading_path": ["Visual rules common to every image", "The image library and its metadata"], "relative_path": "brand/visuals/00-visual-rules-common.md", "start_line": 63}, {"chunk_id": "e78d40b5-bd92-4672-8eb6-72a88ca8639d", "content": "### `restrictions`: check it before every use

Read `restrictions` before you use an image, every time, including images you have used before. Restrictions are added after an image enters the library, so last quarter's check does not count.

The field is free text, written by whoever had the reason. There is no fixed vocabulary, so read the sentence instead of searching for a keyword. Three kinds of note turn up in practice:

- **Retirement.** The image is deprecated and must not be used. Some retired files look entirely normal in the grid and carry no other sign. Their tags and titles may even look current.
- **A limited context.** The image may be used in the named context and nowhere else. A note limiting an image to internal use keeps it out of anything a customer, a prospect or the press will see, and that includes sales decks.
- **A person or place.** Something about who or what is shown has changed.

A restriction binds even when the image would be perfect, when a senior person asks for it, and when you found it already published somewhere. If you think one is out of date, ask Brand to change the record. Do not use the image and sort it out later.

An empty `restrictions` field means nobody has recorded a limit. It does not mean the image is on brand. The field is one check among several, and the current-identity rule above still has to pass on your own judgment.

If `restrictions` and `tags` seem to disagree, `restrictions` wins. If `restrictions` and `description` disagree, stop and ask.

", "document_id": "7393a98e-d420-4e3a-a620-f4bf13834b9d", "end_line": 97, "heading_path": ["Visual rules common to every image", "The image library and its metadata", "restrictions: check it before every use"], "relative_path": "brand/visuals/00-visual-rules-common.md", "start_line": 82}, {"chunk_id": "1579ded5-3a28-44a8-9e3d-df0fd1a0b603", "content": "### `background`

Three values.

- `transparent`: no ground at all. The image takes on whatever is behind it, which is why `safe_on` matters so much for these files.
- `solid`: a flat ground is part of the file, such as a logo on its panel or a hero illustration on Tallow.
- `scene`: the image has its own environment, as every photograph does. You never cut a scene out of its background, and we do not mask people or equipment out of photos.

A file marked `transparent` should be previewed on the actual ground before it ships. A bright fringe can look fine on one ground and show on another.

", "document_id": "7393a98e-d420-4e3a-a620-f4bf13834b9d", "end_line": 107, "heading_path": ["Visual rules common to every image", "The image library and its metadata", "background"], "relative_path": "brand/visuals/00-visual-rules-common.md", "start_line": 98}, {"chunk_id": "1ffbbb49-f324-4941-ad03-c87996d8ac96", "content": "### `safe_on`

Three values, each describing the ground the image is designed to sit on.

- `light`: Tallow and other pale grounds only.
- `dark`: Soot and other deep grounds only.
- `any`: holds up on both.

Treat `safe_on` as a limit, the same way you treat `restrictions`. A `light` image on a dark layout is a defect even if you can still more or less see it. The layout's ground is what matters: a dark band halfway down a light page is a dark ground. When an image sits on a photo, or on Ember or Whetstone, neither word applies directly. Use a `solid` version, or test it and show Brand.

", "document_id": "7393a98e-d420-4e3a-a620-f4bf13834b9d", "end_line": 117, "heading_path": ["Visual rules common to every image", "The image library and its metadata", "safe_on"], "relative_path": "brand/visuals/00-visual-rules-common.md", "start_line": 108}, {"chunk_id": "7bd9df56-982b-4dd6-b3f7-e2c369f80b23", "content": "### `variant_of`

If the record points to a parent, or other records point at this one, you have siblings. Look at them before you decide the image does not work. The version for your ground often already exists.

", "document_id": "7393a98e-d420-4e3a-a620-f4bf13834b9d", "end_line": 121, "heading_path": ["Visual rules common to every image", "The image library and its metadata", "variant_of"], "relative_path": "brand/visuals/00-visual-rules-common.md", "start_line": 118}, {"chunk_id": "76df2e0e-6e05-4285-bede-8b07fece0fb3", "content": "## Picking an image: the order

1. Decide the category and read that page.
2. Decide the content type and read that page.
3. Search the library. Search by description and by a few different words, since tags are uneven.
4. Open the record. Read `restrictions` and `usage_rights` first, then `background`, `safe_on` and size.
5. Look at the picture itself at full size against the current identity. Metadata does not catch everything.
6. Check it against the rest of the layout, on the real ground.
7. Add it to the draft with its `id` noted in the review comment, so Brand can trace it.

", "document_id": "7393a98e-d420-4e3a-a620-f4bf13834b9d", "end_line": 131, "heading_path": ["Visual rules common to every image", "Picking an image: the order"], "relative_path": "brand/visuals/00-visual-rules-common.md", "start_line": 122}, {"chunk_id": "41577904-d665-4bee-853c-6e0e7d81c3fe", "content": "## Three picks, worked through

**A blog post on draining nodes before an upgrade.** The writer finds a warm photo of a rack door. The title and tags look right and `restrictions` is empty. At full size, the photo is clean and it passes. It needs a crop, so the writer checks `width` and `height` first and confirms the focal point stays in frame.

**A dark section on a pricing comparison page.** The designer drops in a spot illustration that looked good on the last page. The record says `background: transparent` and `safe_on: light`, so it fails on this band. The record has no `variant_of`, but another record points at it as a parent, and that sibling is `safe_on: dark`. Problem solved in two minutes.

**A customer webinar invitation.** The perfect team photo has a line in `restrictions` that the writer almost skipped, because the thumbnail looked fine and the image had been used on the website last year. The line changes the answer. The image stays out, whatever last year's page did, and the writer picks again.

", "document_id": "7393a98e-d420-4e3a-a620-f4bf13834b9d", "end_line": 139, "heading_path": ["Visual rules common to every image", "Three picks, worked through"], "relative_path": "brand/visuals/00-visual-rules-common.md", "start_line": 132}, {"chunk_id": "dce37ce3-fd82-47df-a26e-44c4f3ee9a0e", "content": "## Asking for something new

If the library has nothing suitable, do not borrow from the web, do not pull an image from a past deck, and do not take it from a teammate's desktop. Files outside the library have no record and nobody can check their rights.

Requests go to the brand designers through the design queue with the placement, the deadline and one sentence on what the image should show. Allow five working days for illustration and more for photography that needs a shoot. Anything made for you gets a metadata record before it ships.

", "document_id": "7393a98e-d420-4e3a-a620-f4bf13834b9d", "end_line": 145, "heading_path": ["Visual rules common to every image", "Asking for something new"], "relative_path": "brand/visuals/00-visual-rules-common.md", "start_line": 140}, {"chunk_id": "e3c0ef0e-e63f-4f78-8f60-5c42511434dd", "content": "## Review

Brand reviews every new image and every first use of a library image in paid, press and homepage work. Anything else can ship on the owner's own check against this page, and Brand samples it monthly. Pull anything that fails the sample, even if it has already gone out.

Legal review is separate. It looks at claims, customer marks and consent. A pass from Legal is not a pass from Brand, and the other way around.
", "document_id": "7393a98e-d420-4e3a-a620-f4bf13834b9d", "end_line": 150, "heading_path": ["Visual rules common to every image", "Review"], "relative_path": "brand/visuals/00-visual-rules-common.md", "start_line": 146}, {"chunk_id": "8dd6c955-a13b-4185-a4fd-f44638a66137", "content": "# Image accessibility

Web lead's notes, cleaned up by Brand in May 2026 after the customer procurement questionnaire asked us about this and we had no document to point to.

", "document_id": "4894ce77-85f4-41f8-b34d-769eb2701e6c", "end_line": 4, "heading_path": ["Image accessibility"], "relative_path": "brand/visuals/accessibility.md", "start_line": 1}, {"chunk_id": "c6394c1c-58a9-4ee0-8f7e-d115ca33d2d6", "content": "## Alt text on every image

Every image has alt text. This covers blog images, email images, landing pages, social uploads where the platform offers the field, and images in PDFs. The author of the piece writes it, because the designer usually does not know why the image is there.

Write what the reader would lose if the image failed to load. One or two plain sentences, under about 125 characters when you can manage it. Skip "image of" and "picture of". Do not stuff keywords. Do not paste the `description` field from the library: that describes the file, and alt text describes what the image is doing in this piece.

| Image | Bad | Good |
|---|---|---|
| Photo | "Engineer, Kubernetes, security, on-call, data center" | "An engineer reads a terminal in a dim equipment room." |
| Product screenshot | "Screenshot of dashboard" | "Quenchline shows one pod isolated, with network access removed and the process frozen." |
| Chart | "Bar chart" | "Median time to contain a runtime incident is 7.4 hours. Wickhold Containment Report 2026." |
| Logo | "logo.png" | "Wickhold logo" |
| Illustration | "Decorative graphic" | "A cut-paper wick with a single small Ember flame." |

Charts and screenshots carry the finding in the alt text, and the reader should not need the picture to get the number. If the chart has more than about four values, put the values in a table or the body copy under it and let the alt text state the point.

Any text set on an image must also appear in the alt text or the surrounding copy. Screen readers cannot read a stat card.

The "every image" part holds for decorative images too. If an image truly adds nothing, the first question is why it is in the piece. Background textures set in CSS are not images for this purpose and need no alt.

", "document_id": "4894ce77-85f4-41f8-b34d-769eb2701e6c", "end_line": 24, "heading_path": ["Image accessibility", "Alt text on every image"], "relative_path": "brand/visuals/accessibility.md", "start_line": 5}, {"chunk_id": "5bce8648-d3e6-4352-a0ff-0023d9af46b9", "content": "## Contrast: 4.5:1 for text

Text on any image or graphic meets at least 4.5:1 against what is directly behind it. We apply the same floor to all sizes, including large headlines. A designer will point out that the web standard relaxes for large type. We know. The single number is easier to check, and a stat card shrinks to thumbnail size in a feed, where large type stops being large. This floor governs images. Layouts follow the logo and color addendum.

Measured ratios for the palette:

| Pair | Ratio | Text allowed? |
|---|---|---|
| Soot on Tallow | 15.5:1 | Yes |
| Tallow on Soot | 15.5:1 | Yes |
| Whetstone on Tallow | 4.8:1 | Yes |
| Verdigris on Soot | 4.5:1 | Yes, just. Test your export |
| Ember on Tallow | 4.1:1 | No |
| Soot on Ember | 3.8:1 | No |
| Ember on Soot | 3.8:1 | No |
| Tallow on Ember | 4.1:1 | No |
| Verdigris on Tallow | 3.4:1 | No |
| Whetstone on Soot | 3.2:1 | No |

This surprises people: Ember does not carry text on our grounds, and no text sits on Ember in an image. Ember is for shapes, rules and the focal element. Headlines on Tallow are Soot. Headlines on Soot are Tallow.

Over a photo, measure against the lightest spot behind the letters for Tallow text and the darkest spot for Soot text. An even-looking dark photo often has one bright lamp right under the word. If the text fails anywhere, put it on a solid Soot or Tallow panel. Do not add a gradient scrim: our illustration and graphic language has no gradients, and scrims tend to fail at their edges anyway.

", "document_id": "4894ce77-85f4-41f8-b34d-769eb2701e6c", "end_line": 47, "heading_path": ["Image accessibility", "Contrast: 4.5:1 for text"], "relative_path": "brand/visuals/accessibility.md", "start_line": 25}, {"chunk_id": "e7537153-760e-4f01-98ec-d00c9d011288", "content": "## Color alone

Do not use color as the only signal. Ember and Verdigris are close in lightness and can merge for a reader with red-green color blindness. Label things directly.

", "document_id": "4894ce77-85f4-41f8-b34d-769eb2701e6c", "end_line": 51, "heading_path": ["Image accessibility", "Color alone"], "relative_path": "brand/visuals/accessibility.md", "start_line": 48}, {"chunk_id": "d69ba9db-bd4e-4fc7-ac14-36e503e1b95e", "content": "## Motion

Looping GIFs stop after three loops, or ship as static. Nothing flashes more than three times a second. A product demo clip on a landing page has a pause control and does not autoplay with sound.

", "document_id": "4894ce77-85f4-41f8-b34d-769eb2701e6c", "end_line": 55, "heading_path": ["Image accessibility", "Motion"], "relative_path": "brand/visuals/accessibility.md", "start_line": 52}, {"chunk_id": "a9d334b2-f0f5-434d-abf2-0a43a5379762", "content": "## Checks before publishing

- Alt text present and written for this placement
- Text on image measured, with the worst spot checked
- Image still makes sense at 320px wide
- Meaning does not depend on color alone
", "document_id": "4894ce77-85f4-41f8-b34d-769eb2701e6c", "end_line": 61, "heading_path": ["Image accessibility", "Checks before publishing"], "relative_path": "brand/visuals/accessibility.md", "start_line": 56}, {"chunk_id": "9eeb0cca-0fab-4d0b-aba9-a395e700120f", "content": "# Blog hero images

Content team working rules, June 2026.

**Every blog post has one hero. It is a 16:9 illustration or photo. It is never a dashboard.**

Product UI in the hero looks like an ad on top of an article, and the detail goes illegible at the size most people see it, which is the preview card. If a post is about a product screen, put the screenshot in the body, at a size where it can be read.

", "document_id": "ee1e2860-3009-43a3-a2f8-38f054e36600", "end_line": 8, "heading_path": ["Blog hero images"], "relative_path": "brand/visuals/by-content-type/blog-hero.md", "start_line": 1}, {"chunk_id": "0d442c6b-7865-458b-8c5e-ab89f2abdd35", "content": "## Narrower than the category pages

Not everything in the illustration category qualifies here:

- **Hero illustrations only.** A spot illustration is transparent and square, and it sits inside body copy. Set as a hero, it leaves a small object floating in a wide band, so it is out.
- **No abstract backgrounds.** They have no focal point on their own, and a hero has no type set over it.
- **Tallow or Soot, matched to the post.** Illustration category rules allow either. For blog heroes, default to Tallow. Use Soot for incident retrospectives and long technical posts, so that the list page has some rhythm.

And from photography:

- **Landscape only.** Portrait photos in the library cannot become 16:9 without losing most of the frame.
- **A person is allowed as the subject, but the post has to be about the work** and not a staff profile.

No text on the hero at all, including the post title. The blog template sets the title in live type below the image. Older posts had titles burned into the image, and they looked wrong in every preview card that also printed the title.

", "document_id": "ee1e2860-3009-43a3-a2f8-38f054e36600", "end_line": 23, "heading_path": ["Blog hero images", "Narrower than the category pages"], "relative_path": "brand/visuals/by-content-type/blog-hero.md", "start_line": 9}, {"chunk_id": "d4925866-8875-4cbd-9a6f-d1368287a31e", "content": "## Size and crop

Export at 1600x900. Most library heroes and photos are 3:2, so you will lose some height. Crop from the top and bottom, then check that the focal point has survived. A hero illustration's focal element usually sits off center and the quiet part can go. Some platforms crop preview cards further, so keep the focal point out of the outer tenth of the frame.

Do not upscale. A 1536-wide source enlarged to 1600 is about the limit, and it should look clean at full size.

", "document_id": "ee1e2860-3009-43a3-a2f8-38f054e36600", "end_line": 29, "heading_path": ["Blog hero images", "Size and crop"], "relative_path": "brand/visuals/by-content-type/blog-hero.md", "start_line": 24}, {"chunk_id": "6b2f30da-423b-4eae-8725-3f1eae6d3b11", "content": "## Choosing by post type

| Post | Hero |
|---|---|
| Founder essay, signed by Maren | Photo of a working room, or a quiet illustration |
| Technical post by Dov or the engineering team | Infrastructure photo or a concept illustration tied to the mechanism |
| Customer story | Photo from that customer's site if released, otherwise an illustration. Never a stand-in photo that implies it is their site |
| Containment Report findings | Illustration. Save the charts for the body |
| Comparison post | Neutral illustration. No competitor logos or product screens |
| Incident analysis or a post about a breach | Quiet illustration without flame, or an empty-room photo. Keep it plain |

The hero is chosen for the idea in the post. A post on default containment policies should not get a generic "engineer with laptop". Find the one object that matches: a tray under a wick, a closed rack door, a hand on a breaker.

", "document_id": "ee1e2860-3009-43a3-a2f8-38f054e36600", "end_line": 42, "heading_path": ["Blog hero images", "Choosing by post type"], "relative_path": "brand/visuals/by-content-type/blog-hero.md", "start_line": 30}, {"chunk_id": "bd87798f-d977-4194-91d7-66f449484b7d", "content": "## Avoiding repeats

Check the last ten posts on the blog before you commit. The same image twice in a month makes the blog look thin, and readers on the index page see them side by side. Since a hero image goes out in the social card by default, check the record's `restrictions` as you would for social use.

", "document_id": "ee1e2860-3009-43a3-a2f8-38f054e36600", "end_line": 46, "heading_path": ["Blog hero images", "Avoiding repeats"], "relative_path": "brand/visuals/by-content-type/blog-hero.md", "start_line": 43}, {"chunk_id": "fd73b325-8d36-4f14-b28d-2e03856bb8dd", "content": "## Open graph card

The hero doubles as the social preview card unless a separate card is uploaded. Look at the preview before publishing, as the crop differs from the page. If the preview loses the focal point, upload a separate crop.

", "document_id": "ee1e2860-3009-43a3-a2f8-38f054e36600", "end_line": 50, "heading_path": ["Blog hero images", "Open graph card"], "relative_path": "brand/visuals/by-content-type/blog-hero.md", "start_line": 47}, {"chunk_id": "43065efb-c883-495a-baa3-a128ed3a27b6", "content": "## Series and guest posts

A multi-part series uses one hero object across all its parts, changed slightly each time. Guest posts from customers follow the same rules, and a guest's own company image only runs if Brand has checked it. Never accept a stock image from a contributor.

", "document_id": "ee1e2860-3009-43a3-a2f8-38f054e36600", "end_line": 54, "heading_path": ["Blog hero images", "Series and guest posts"], "relative_path": "brand/visuals/by-content-type/blog-hero.md", "start_line": 51}, {"chunk_id": "785f8389-2bfc-49d0-8c8c-858c1dfe7379", "content": "## Credit and caption

No caption on heroes. No credit line unless the record's `attribution` calls for one.

", "document_id": "ee1e2860-3009-43a3-a2f8-38f054e36600", "end_line": 58, "heading_path": ["Blog hero images", "Credit and caption"], "relative_path": "brand/visuals/by-content-type/blog-hero.md", "start_line": 55}, {"chunk_id": "bfb82499-dbaa-4829-975f-6158d7cdb131", "content": "## Who picks

The post's author proposes and the blog editor approves. The first use of a new hero in a homepage feature goes through Brand review.
", "document_id": "ee1e2860-3009-43a3-a2f8-38f054e36600", "end_line": 61, "heading_path": ["Blog hero images", "Who picks"], "relative_path": "brand/visuals/by-content-type/blog-hero.md", "start_line": 59}, {"chunk_id": "02716bff-8a50-4874-8f7a-09a8932d9324", "content": "# LinkedIn images

Social lead's notes, updated August 2026.

", "document_id": "beef8954-7afc-41b9-af69-a34fc60372d1", "end_line": 4, "heading_path": ["LinkedIn images"], "relative_path": "brand/visuals/by-content-type/linkedin-image.md", "start_line": 1}, {"chunk_id": "20fa3480-8a74-41f5-93fe-a4a0faa9ff11", "content": "## The spec

- **1200x627.** Export at exactly this size. Anything else gets cropped by the platform, and the crop rarely helps
- **At most seven words of overlay text**
- **Overlay text is added in design**, as live type in the template, over a finished image

Seven words means seven, counted the plain way. A hyphenated word is one word, and a number is one word. The logo does not count. A source line does count, so most stat images move the source into the post copy, which is where we want it anyway.

The seven-word cap narrows what the social graphics rules allow. A stat card on any other surface can carry a measure line and a source. On LinkedIn it gets the number and the short label only.

| Overlay | Words | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| Small fires stay small. | 4 | Good |
| Median time to contain: 7.4 hours | 6 | Good, source in the post |
| 11 minutes, down from 4 hours | 6 | Good, with Lowmoor named in the post |
| Contain first. Then find out what happened. | 7 | Good |
| What Wickhold learned from surveying 412 platform and security leaders | 10 | Too long |
| Is your team ready for a runtime incident? | 8 | Too long, and it is a question |

", "document_id": "beef8954-7afc-41b9-af69-a34fc60372d1", "end_line": 23, "heading_path": ["LinkedIn images", "The spec"], "relative_path": "brand/visuals/by-content-type/linkedin-image.md", "start_line": 5}, {"chunk_id": "fb8ebfa4-edf7-47b6-9fc6-f7fc19ed13b6", "content": "## What goes in the frame

Use, in rough order of how well they have done for us:

1. A photo of real work, with no overlay at all
2. A stat card from the social templates. Quote cards rarely fit the cap
3. A short product crop showing one action, large enough to read in the feed
4. A hero illustration, cropped

Library images are 3:2, so a 1200x627 crop loses about a fifth of the height. Keep the focal point near the vertical center. Spot illustrations should sit on a solid Tallow or Soot layout from the template. They are transparent and LinkedIn will show them on its own background if you upload them as they are.

Do not run overlay text across a photo's focal point. Text goes on a solid band or in the quiet side of the frame.

", "document_id": "beef8954-7afc-41b9-af69-a34fc60372d1", "end_line": 36, "heading_path": ["LinkedIn images", "What goes in the frame"], "relative_path": "brand/visuals/by-content-type/linkedin-image.md", "start_line": 24}, {"chunk_id": "ff69da54-653c-40e9-8d69-584ac2e79e5e", "content": "## By account

**Company page.** Follows all of the above. Logo present on designed images, absent on plain photos.

**Founder accounts.** Maren's and Dov's posts take a plain photo or no image. Designed cards with a company logo look like an ad under a personal post, so skip them. No overlay text on founder images unless Maren asks for it.

**Staff.** Anyone can use the approved templates. Reshare the file as it is.

", "document_id": "beef8954-7afc-41b9-af69-a34fc60372d1", "end_line": 44, "heading_path": ["LinkedIn images", "By account"], "relative_path": "brand/visuals/by-content-type/linkedin-image.md", "start_line": 37}, {"chunk_id": "c28e7438-46d7-471e-b55d-ea5418751c6c", "content": "## Document posts and video

PDF document posts are off the plan, for the same reasons as carousels. Native video follows the screenshot rules for captures. A title frame counts as an image and falls under the seven-word cap.

", "document_id": "beef8954-7afc-41b9-af69-a34fc60372d1", "end_line": 48, "heading_path": ["LinkedIn images", "Document posts and video"], "relative_path": "brand/visuals/by-content-type/linkedin-image.md", "start_line": 45}, {"chunk_id": "d97fd5bf-b314-4163-8e1f-2521813ecbb0", "content": "## Timing against the event calendar

Dated images age badly. A card that names a date comes down from the scheduled queue the moment the date moves. After the event, do not reuse it. Set `restrictions` on the record when you file it, as with any time-limited card.

", "document_id": "beef8954-7afc-41b9-af69-a34fc60372d1", "end_line": 52, "heading_path": ["LinkedIn images", "Timing against the event calendar"], "relative_path": "brand/visuals/by-content-type/linkedin-image.md", "start_line": 49}, {"chunk_id": "544d6eb7-4e7d-4af7-9e11-a9697aa1e6e9", "content": "## Series that have worked

Monthly "from the Containment Report" posts with one number and no other decoration. Plain photos in Field Day recaps, chosen with the people rules in mind. Short "what changed in this release" crops. What has not worked: anything that looks like a slide. If a LinkedIn image looks as if it came from a deck, redo it.

", "document_id": "beef8954-7afc-41b9-af69-a34fc60372d1", "end_line": 56, "heading_path": ["LinkedIn images", "Series that have worked"], "relative_path": "brand/visuals/by-content-type/linkedin-image.md", "start_line": 53}, {"chunk_id": "4cc79ef9-1bab-442c-9b23-f5c6c5ec0376", "content": "## Checks

- 1200x627 exactly
- Count the words
- Overlay legible at phone width
- Image record read, including `restrictions`

The picture should still make sense with the post text collapsed, since the image is often all a reader sees before "see more".

The most common error in the last quarter was a logo dropped on without checking the ground. The second was a stat shortened until it no longer said what the source said. If shortening changes the meaning, use a different stat or use no overlay.

Wickhold is someone who has been paged more often than you have and is not going to bring it up.

**Unhurried.** Nothing in our copy is urgent. A page that hurries the reader is using the same trick as the alert fatigue they came to us to get away from.

**Exact.** "Isolated the pod's network" beats "took action". "220 nodes" beats "at scale". If two engineers would argue over what a sentence means, it isn't finished.

**Unimpressed by itself.** The product is useful. Copy that gasps at it reads as though the writer has not seen it fail. We have seen it fail, and the release notes say so.

**On your side of the pager.** The reader is a peer on the same rota, and we write to them as someone who could take the next shift. No lecturing, no "did you know", no explaining Kubernetes to people who run it.

When the character slips, it usually slips into one of four people:

- **The hero.** Rushes in, saves the day, gets the credit. Early rebrand drafts leaned on firefighters and helmets until Maren pointed out that a firefighter arriving means it already went badly. The customer's on-call team is the competent party in every story we tell.
- **The prophet.** Sees doom everywhere and sells shelter from it. The whole security industry's default register, which makes it invisible to the people we want to reach.
- **The buddy.** "Hey there, Kubernetes friends." Nobody paged at 3am wants a pal.
- **The analyst.** "In today's rapidly evolving threat landscape." Sentences with no one in them. If nothing would change when the paragraph is deleted, delete it.

No threat-actor drama. No ticking clocks.

The rule is simple to state and gets broken constantly, because fear copy is the easiest copy in security to write. It covers attackers portrayed as characters with motives and nicknames, anything of the "while you read this" kind, countdowns, "it's only a matter of time", "every second counts", and any sentence that asks the reader to imagine the phone call to the board. Our readers carry a pager. They do not need help imagining it.

Give the same fact without the dread.

Bad: "Attackers are already inside your cluster, and the clock is ticking."

Good: "41% of platform teams need more than six hours to contain a runtime incident [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report]."

The second sentence is more uncomfortable than the first, and it did not raise its voice. Trust the number to do that work.

Breach references have their own rules in the claims document. Read them before you mention one.

Something will get through. Every serious engineer already knows this, and the companies who claim otherwise are talking to someone else. Wickhold's position is that the useful question is how far a failure gets and how fast it stops spreading. The whole product line follows from that, and so does most of our vocabulary. ", "document_id": "17287b9b-a53b-4506-b269-2d0c53d38767", "end_line": 60, "heading_path": ["Wickhold voice and tone", "What Wickhold believes", "Containment is the whole argument"], "relative_path": "brand/voice/voice-and-tone-2026.md", "start_line": 57}, {"chunk_id": "bc78b090-211c-4c83-92b8-ef866c9adc03", "content": "### Say the number, then stop

Claims carry a figure and a source. No adjective stacks.

"Fast" is not a claim. "A fast, powerful, highly scalable runtime platform" is three non-claims in a row. Write the number, say where it came from, and end the sentence. The urge to add a second sentence explaining why the number is impressive is the urge to resist. A reader who needs that sentence is the wrong reader; a reader who doesn't will think less of us for it.

Bad: "Lowmoor Credit Union saw an incredible, game-changing reduction in response times."

Good: "Lowmoor Credit Union cut time to contain from 4 hours to 11 minutes across 220 nodes."

Bad: "Quenchline is extremely lightweight and blazingly quick."

Good: "Wickhold Quenchline contains a known-bad process in a median of 38 seconds in Wickhold lab benchmarks, 2026."

If there is no figure, there is usually no claim, and the honest move is to describe what the product does in plain mechanical terms. "Isolates a pod's network" needs no number and no source. It's a description. "Industry-leading isolation" needs both and has neither.

One of the company values, and the one marketing finds hardest. Every product we sell has an edge. Wickhold Evenburn finds drift and exposure paths; it does not contain anything. There are two voices at Wickhold, and they have one hard line between them.

**Founder voice is first person singular, and it is signed.** Maren writes as "I". Her posts carry her name. She gets to have feelings and doubts, tell a story from a bad night in 2017, and be wrong in public. Dov's technical posts work the same way and are signed "Dov".

**Brand voice never says "I" or "we think".** Website, product pages, company LinkedIn, the company X account, email, decks, reports: no first person singular, ever. "We believe", "we feel" and "in our view" are "we think" in different shoes, and they go too.

**Brand voice uses "Wickhold" or "we" for facts only.** Things that happened, things that are true of the company, things a lawyer could check.

| Fine in brand voice | Not in brand voice |
|---|---|
| We renewed SOC 2 Type II in January 2026. | We think SOC 2 matters. |
| Wickhold serves more than 140 customers. | I've talked to a lot of platform teams. |
| Containment is where incidents are won or lost. | We believe containment is where incidents are won or lost. |

The third row is the useful one. Brand voice still holds opinions. It states them as flat sentences, the way the on-call lead does, and lets the reader disagree. "We think" adds nothing except a hedge.

Practicalities. Nobody else writes as "I" in Wickhold content. Kofi's developer posts and anything from the wider team run in brand voice under a byline, because a byline is credit and a founder post is a person speaking for themselves. Customer quotes are quotes and say whatever was approved. If the content team drafts for Maren, she reads it and changes it before her name goes on, and a post that she has not read does not go out. In the spring a joint Maren-and-Dov byline was tried on one post; "I" became unreadable after two paragraphs, so that was dropped. One author per post.

", "document_id": "17287b9b-a53b-4506-b269-2d0c53d38767", "end_line": 104, "heading_path": ["Wickhold voice and tone", "Founder voice and brand voice"], "relative_path": "brand/voice/voice-and-tone-2026.md", "start_line": 85}, {"chunk_id": "1b2ec0a3-937b-43d7-a777-88143fa3b565", "content": "## Tone by channel

The voice stays the same. How much of it you get changes with the room.

**Landing pages.** The flattest we get. Mechanical, confident, short. The reader is deciding whether to spend ten more minutes, so tell them what the thing does on a cluster and let them go. "Wickhold Quenchline isolates the pod, freezes the process or drains the node, then writes down what it did."

**Blog.** The most room to think. Brand-voice posts walk through how something fails. Dov's posts can argue, and they should. A good post leaves the reader able to do one thing they could not do before, even if they never buy. Avoid the summary paragraph at the end. If the post worked, the reader was there.

**LinkedIn.** The company page is brand voice. Founder posts are where the personality lives. A post runs about 200 words, which suits one story and one point. Write as a person with a job, not a thought leader: no line breaks after every sentence, no "here's what I learned", no lists of lessons from an outage.

**X.** One fact, or one observation, in a dry tone. The account does not chase the news and does not reply to arguments about vendors. It's fine for a post to be plain. "The median time to contain a runtime incident is 7.4 hours [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report]. That is most of a night shift."

**Email.** One person writing to one person who is busy. Say why you are writing in the first sentence. Assume it is being read on a phone in a hallway. No "I hope this finds you well", and since these are brand emails, no "I" at all unless Maren signed it. Customer notices are the exception to everything else in this list and sound like the incident channel at the top of this document.

**Product UI and error text.** The closest thing we have to pure voice. What happened, what state things are in, what to do. "Containment action failed on node `ip-10-2-14-7`: agent unreachable. The pod is still running. Retry or drain the node." Chirpy empty states were tried in 2025 and came out after a customer saw one during a real incident.

**Case studies.** Third person, numbers up front, the customer's team as the subject of most sentences. Enough detail about their environment that a peer recognizes it. A case study that could describe any customer describes none of them.

**Release notes.** Past tense, specific, no selling. A bug we fixed is described as a bug.

**Press.** Third person, plain, one idea per release. The quote from Maren is the only place with any warmth, and she writes it herself.

Humor depends on the audience, see each persona.

The personas hold the working rules for each reader, including what goes first. What follows is only the register, meaning how the voice sounds once you have chosen your content.

**CISOs.** Level and measured. Assume the reader will forward your paragraph to an audit committee without editing it, and write something they can forward. Risk, time and board language are their native terms: exposure, time to contain, residual risk, ownership. Short sentences, complete ones, no shorthand. Every sentence should survive being read aloud in a room that includes a lawyer.

**Platform engineers.** A good pull-request comment from a colleague you respect. Exact, brief, assumes competence, and shows its working. If there is a YAML snippet that makes the point, the prose can get out of its way. Marketing English reads as noise here and the page will be closed.

**DevSecOps.** These readers sit between the review queue and the pipeline, and they spend their days being the person who says no. Write to someone who is outnumbered: practical, on their side, and specific about what lands in their queue and what stays out of it.

**Compliance leads.** Careful nouns. This reader will notice the difference between "supports" and "meets", and will quote you. Their persona is still being written, so if the piece is aimed mainly at them, ask Noor before guessing.

**Customers mid-incident.** Pure 3am voice. Nothing about the product, nothing about the relationship, no reassurance that isn't backed by a fact. What we see, what we've done, when the next update comes.

**Finance and procurement.** They read a small part of what we write and they read it closely. Plain sentences, the price in the standard form, the terms where they expect them. Anything that sounds like enthusiasm reads to them as a negotiating position.

**Journalists.** Assume no interest in the product and real interest in what is happening to teams. Offer the finding, the method and a person to talk to. Don't send them a story with a hook in it; they have their own.

**Candidates and the community.** Warmer, plainer, and allowed to mention that the work is interesting. The same no-drama rules hold. Nobody here is a rockstar.

We will have our own bad days: a bad agent release, a late fix, a false containment that drained a node it should have left alone. The values cover this before anything else does. Say what happened. Contain first. Admit limits. Leave it better for the next on-call.

In practice:

- Lead with what happened to the customer's systems, in their terms.
- Use "we" and an active verb. "We shipped a policy update that drained nodes it should not have." "An issue occurred" is not a sentence we publish.
- Apologize once, plainly, in one short sentence. Then get on with the facts.
- Say what is still unknown.
- Say when the next update comes, and hit that time even if there's nothing new.

Dov signs off anything technical. Priit Salonen reads anything that touches a contract. Nobody in marketing edits the facts for tone.

", "document_id": "17287b9b-a53b-4506-b269-2d0c53d38767", "end_line": 172, "heading_path": ["Wickhold voice and tone", "When the news is ours"], "relative_path": "brand/voice/voice-and-tone-2026.md", "start_line": 159}, {"chunk_id": "1fd4a899-36f9-4680-a5bd-e12cfd218f0d", "content": "## One fact, three rooms

The same pair of numbers, set for three readers. The facts stay fixed and the weight moves.

On a landing page, where the reader is deciding whether to keep going:

> The median time to contain a runtime incident is 7.4 hours [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report]. Wickhold Quenchline contains a known-bad process in a median of 38 seconds in Wickhold lab benchmarks, 2026.

In a note to a CISO, where the number has to fit a conversation about risk:

> The median time to contain a runtime incident is 7.4 hours [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report]. Your team's own figure is the one to bring to the risk committee.

In a post for platform engineers, where the first response to a lab figure is suspicion:

> Wickhold Quenchline contains a known-bad process in a median of 38 seconds in Wickhold lab benchmarks, 2026. Your cluster is not our lab. Run it in observe mode and read what it would have done.

None of the three is more honest than the others. Each one hands the reader the number in the form they can use.

", "document_id": "17287b9b-a53b-4506-b269-2d0c53d38767", "end_line": 190, "heading_path": ["Wickhold voice and tone", "One fact, three rooms"], "relative_path": "brand/voice/voice-and-tone-2026.md", "start_line": 173}, {"chunk_id": "1157e9ca-6b0f-49f2-9b39-5f3c606b38f5", "content": "## Subjects that pull the voice off course

Some topics drag writers back toward the register the rebrand left behind. These are the ones reviewers see most.

**AI agents.** Wickhold Leashgate, in early access, attracts the worst habits in the building, because the whole market is shouting about agents. Treat an agent as a workload with credentials and questionable judgment. Talk about tool calls, agent identity and the blast radius of an agent. Leave the future of work to other people. Anyone who has run production will recognize the problem from there, and that recognition is worth more than any amount of excitement.

**Compliance.** Dull on purpose. Certification status is a fact with one correct wording, and legal owns that wording. Copy the approved sentence and do not improve it. A nicer phrasing here is how a company ends up saying something untrue.

**Money.** Prices are stated flatly, with no "just", "only" or "starting from". Core is $18 per node per month. The reader can decide how they feel about that.

**Company news.** Funding, awards, headcount. Nobody is thrilled, excited or proud. The Series B was $46M in June 2024; that is a date and a number, and the sentence after it should say what changed for customers. If nothing changed for customers, ask whether the post needs to exist.

**Customers.** They did the work. Lowmoor Credit Union's on-call team runs its own incidents, and the product took one job off their list. Avoid "partnered with", "journey" and anything that casts us as the guide who showed them the way.

**Other approaches.** The voice doesn't sneer. Other kinds of product make real trade-offs, and a colleague would describe them as trade-offs: a heavier agent can see more and costs more on the node. Readers respect the writer who can state the other side accurately. Reviewers will cut anything that sounds like a playground.

**Open source.** Kubernetes, eBPF and Helm were here before us. We are users and we say so. Credit the projects, don't imply we invented the kernel feature, and don't describe a community as an "ecosystem we're proud to be part of".

", "document_id": "17287b9b-a53b-4506-b269-2d0c53d38767", "end_line": 208, "heading_path": ["Wickhold voice and tone", "Subjects that pull the voice off course"], "relative_path": "brand/voice/voice-and-tone-2026.md", "start_line": 191}, {"chunk_id": "383000ed-25fc-4fa8-8a32-0a9cb7da5f80", "content": "## How the sentences go

**Short first.** Most sentences run under twenty words. The long ones earn it by carrying a real sequence of events.

**Verbs do the work.** Name who did what. "Quenchline froze the process" over "the process was frozen". Past tense for incidents, present tense for what the product does.

**End early.** Our most common edit is deleting the last line of a paragraph. Writers tend to add one that restates the point in a nicer rhythm. Readers don't need it. This goes double for the final line of a piece.

**Ration the fire.** The tagline is "Small fires stay small." It carries the metaphor so the copy doesn't have to. A piece gets at most one fire image, and many pieces should have none. Nothing ignites, sparks, blazes or fans the flames. Slow Burn Summit gets to keep its name.

**Plain words for plain things.** "Use", "start", "stop", "run". Reach for the fancier word and the reader assumes something is being hidden.

**Don't argue with the reader's experience.** Telling a platform engineer that alerts are overwhelming is telling them what they had for breakfast. Start from what they know and add something.

", "document_id": "17287b9b-a53b-4506-b269-2d0c53d38767", "end_line": 222, "heading_path": ["Wickhold voice and tone", "How the sentences go"], "relative_path": "brand/voice/voice-and-tone-2026.md", "start_line": 209}, {"chunk_id": "465fccba-1c12-447b-bcf9-71f4083ea5ec", "content": "## What sounds like us

| Sounds like Wickhold | Doesn't |
|---|---|
| Here is what happened. | We're reaching out to share an important update. |
| We don't know yet. | We are actively investigating. |
| That part is still yours. | We've got you covered. |
| Start in observe mode. | Begin your containment journey. |
| It took 11 minutes. | In record time. |
| It's a trade-off. | No compromises. |
| The pod is still running. | Your environment remains protected. |

", "document_id": "17287b9b-a53b-4506-b269-2d0c53d38767", "end_line": 234, "heading_path": ["Wickhold voice and tone", "What sounds like us"], "relative_path": "brand/voice/voice-and-tone-2026.md", "start_line": 223}, {"chunk_id": "7f1c6115-d13c-4954-b8dc-d9d71ce61d60", "content": "## One rewrite, start to finish

A draft that came through in May, lightly disguised:

> We're excited to announce that we think our powerful new drift capabilities will transform how modern teams approach cloud risk, giving you the confidence you need in an increasingly dangerous world.

The edit went like this.

"We're excited to announce" went first. The reader's interest in our excitement is zero.

"We think" is out, because this is brand voice.

"Powerful", "new" and "modern" were doing nothing. Remove them and the sentence gets more honest and no less informative.

"Increasingly dangerous world" is the fear habit, and it also isn't something we can source.

That left "drift capabilities will transform how teams approach cloud risk", which on inspection means nothing. So the reviewer asked the only useful question: what does a person see on the screen? The product manager's answer became the copy.

> Wickhold Evenburn lists the drift in a cluster and ranks it by exposure path, so the fix order is on one page. It does not contain anything at runtime.

That is shorter, it can be checked, and it names an edge. Nobody involved felt that it was a loss.

", "document_id": "17287b9b-a53b-4506-b269-2d0c53d38767", "end_line": 256, "heading_path": ["Wickhold voice and tone", "One rewrite, start to finish"], "relative_path": "brand/voice/voice-and-tone-2026.md", "start_line": 235}, {"chunk_id": "ca1ba113-65da-4917-9655-fa55f8b6ad6f", "content": "## Reading old copy

Pre-2026 material is everywhere: the archive, old decks, the sales team's memory. It sounds different for a reason. The old brand sold watching. It leaned on "always", "every" and "complete", and it got excited in public. A lot of it is competent copy for a company we no longer are.

If you are reusing something from before the rebrand, do not patch the sentences. Take the facts, check that they are still approved, and write it again. Look for these symptoms when reading a draft that someone has recycled: a promise of total coverage, a sentence about seeing with nothing about what happens next, and an excited tone that doesn't match the numbers beside it.

", "document_id": "17287b9b-a53b-4506-b269-2d0c53d38767", "end_line": 262, "heading_path": ["Wickhold voice and tone", "Reading old copy"], "relative_path": "brand/voice/voice-and-tone-2026.md", "start_line": 257}, {"chunk_id": "14a4ed39-6739-4280-b03c-10055a2758db", "content": "## Tried and dropped

The rebrand ran through a lot of ideas. Recording them saves the next person some time.

- **"3am" as a campaign.** A homepage concept with a live clock counting down to the next page. Striking, and a ticking clock in the literal sense. The 3am idea stayed in this document, which is where it belongs: it's how we write, and readers don't need to be told about it.

Then a few checks that catch most problems:

- Can a stranger tell what happened, what is contained and what is next?
- Does each claim have a figure and a source, or is it a plain description of what the product does?
- Is there an "I" or "we think" outside a signed founder piece?
- Does anything rely on the reader being scared?
- What's the last line doing there?

Copy review goes through #brand-review, and Noor or one of the brand team turns it around in two working days. Claims go to Priit Salonen's team and take the time the approved claims set. If a deadline leans on either of those, say so early.

", "document_id": "06fc2e42-e44a-4d3a-9bdf-1663aae5bc1e", "end_line": 4, "heading_path": ["Word list"], "relative_path": "brand/voice/word-list.md", "start_line": 1}, {"chunk_id": "63250d81-fd52-48b4-90ff-f2aea5b27906", "content": "## Banned terms

There are thirteen. They stay out of headlines, body copy, decks, alt text and speaker notes that leave the building. When one shows up in a draft it usually marks the spot where the writer ran out of facts, so deleting it rarely fixes the sentence. Find the fact.

| Term | Why it is out | What to do instead |
|---|---|---|
| seamless | Putting an eBPF agent on every node has seams: a kernel check, a Helm upgrade, a stretch in observe mode. Platform engineers know this and stop reading when told otherwise. | Say what the rollout takes. |
| robust | Strong against what? The word claims a result and skips the test. | Name the failure the thing survived. |
| leverage | A finance word doing a job that "use" does for free. | Use "use". |
| best-in-class | No class, no judge, no source. It cannot pass "say the number, then stop". | Give the figure and where it came from. |
| next-gen | Every product in this market has been next-gen at some point. The word ages the day it ships. | Say what it does on a node today. |
| single pane of glass | Our readers have been sold this pane many times and own several. It also describes watching, and the job here is containing. | Name the screen and what it shows. |
| holistic | Usually covering for a gap. If something spans cloud and cluster, those two words are shorter and checkable. | List what is covered. |
| unlock | Implies the customer's own work was locked up and we hold the key. Drags padlocks into the room as well. | Say what the reader can now do. |
| empower | The readers already have root. Nobody here hands out power. | Say what changed for them, in a verb they would use. |
| cutting-edge | A claim about us, and an undated one. eBPF is well past being new, and that is one reason it is safe to run in production. | Name the technique. |
| game-changing | An incident is nobody's game, and the claim has no number attached. | Give the before and after. |
| prevent all | A promise no security product can keep. Includes "prevents all", which is the same promise with better grammar. | See the verbs below. |
| stop all | Same promise, same problem. A CISO who reads this line once will discount the rest of the page. | See the verbs below. |

The prose test: if a sentence still reads as true after you swap the product for a toaster, it needed a fact and got an adjective.

", "document_id": "06fc2e42-e44a-4d3a-9bdf-1663aae5bc1e", "end_line": 26, "heading_path": ["Word list", "Banned terms"], "relative_path": "brand/voice/word-list.md", "start_line": 5}, {"chunk_id": "64d6d696-ec4f-4e0f-bd79-0d600e9cfca7", "content": "## Preferred terms

**Workload, not asset.** Customers run workloads, and that is the word they use in their own runbooks. "Asset" comes from inventory spreadsheets and suggests a thing that sits still. A workload moves, restarts and misbehaves, which is why it needs a runtime product. Inside the marketing team "asset" still means a blog post or an image file; that use never reaches a customer.

**Contain, limit and slow, rather than prevent.** This is the company's argument in three verbs. Something will go wrong on a Tuesday night regardless of what anyone buys. Wickhold Quenchline contains what is already running. Wickhold Evenburn limits exposure. Wickhold Leashgate limits what an agent can reach. "Slow" is the honest verb when the action buys time and does not end the problem. Also keep "eliminate" and "eradicate" out of it; they are "prevent" in a bigger coat.

Use "contain" only when a containment action actually happens. Detection on its own is detection.

One exception came out of a release-notes review. A line saying a patch prevents a crash in the agent is describing our own bug, so it can stay. The rule covers promises about what happens to customers, and a changelog entry makes none.

**Customers, not clients.** Clients have an account manager and a lunch. Customers run our agent in production and page us. A "client" in the software sense stays: `kubectl` is a client, an email client is a client. "Users" is fine when you mean the people logged in to the console, because a customer is the whole company.

", "document_id": "06fc2e42-e44a-4d3a-9bdf-1663aae5bc1e", "end_line": 38, "heading_path": ["Word list", "Preferred terms"], "relative_path": "brand/voice/word-list.md", "start_line": 27}, {"chunk_id": "ed8f97a1-1b9b-4b82-aabf-5e345010f2ed", "content": "## Not banned, but expect a comment

Reviewers will ask about these. Sometimes the word survives.

- **solution.** Name the product, or say what it does. The word exists to avoid doing either.
- **visibility.** Seeing isn't the job. If the sentence ends at seeing, ask what happens next.
- **real-time.** Fine with a number next to it. Without one it means nothing.
- **AI-powered.** Tells the reader how something was built and nothing about what it does.
- **comprehensive.** Usually untrue, and a reader will go looking for the gap.
- **threat landscape.** A landscape has no one in it. Say which failure you mean.
- **peace of mind.** Nobody on a rota has ever had this.
- **modern.** Compared with what? Say which setup you mean.
- **mission-critical.** To the person on call, everything is.

", "document_id": "06fc2e42-e44a-4d3a-9bdf-1663aae5bc1e", "end_line": 52, "heading_path": ["Word list", "Not banned, but expect a comment"], "relative_path": "brand/voice/word-list.md", "start_line": 39}, {"chunk_id": "403da354-2435-4bf0-9f6b-a39610835fdf", "content": "## Off the list

- **"Platform".** On the first draft in January, then removed. Half our readers are platform engineers.
- **"Blast radius".** Someone proposed banning it as fear language. It stays, because engineers use it flatly and "blast radius of an agent" is how Leashgate work gets scoped.
- **A Slack bot that flagged banned terms.** Tried for a month in the spring. It flagged `client` in every Kubernetes snippet and nobody read its messages after the first week. Removed. Reviewers catch these now.

To add or remove a term, make the case in #brand-review with a real sentence from a real draft. Kofi Anselm's team has a veto on anything engineers actually say.

Noor Eskelund, May 2026

"af2f7190-800c-4853-bae8-1c9d3d57bed5", "relative_path": "brand/channels/linkedin-playbook.md", "heading_path": ["LinkedIn playbook"], "start_line": 1, "end_line": 6, "content": "# LinkedIn playbook

Noor Eskelund. Last edit 12 August 2026, after the Leashgate early access posts. Ask in the brand channel before you ask me by email.

LinkedIn is the one channel where CISOs, platform leads and our own hiring pipeline all look at the same feed. Most of what we post there is read on a phone, between meetings, by someone who has never heard of us. Write for that person.

"}, {"chunk_id": "f1e93386-bd9e-4240-9294-b61ce8701dec", "document_id": "af2f7190-800c-4853-bae8-1c9d3d57bed5", "relative_path": "brand/channels/linkedin-playbook.md", "heading_path": ["LinkedIn playbook", "Who posts"], "start_line": 7, "end_line": 16, "content": "## Who posts

**Company page.** Marketing runs it. Two or three posts a week, Tuesday to Thursday, usually mid-morning Mountain time. Fridays stayed on the calendar through most of 2025 and did nothing, so they came off.

**Maren and Dov.** They post from their own profiles when they have something to say. Marketing can draft, but they rewrite. Do not schedule on their behalf without a yes in writing, and do not reply to comments as them. If a draft of Maren's has been sitting for two weeks, drop it. She has decided.

**Kofi and the DevRel team.** Kofi posts from his own profile about conference talks, open-source eBPF work and whatever broke in the demo cluster. He does not need brand review for those unless a post carries a customer name, a product claim or a number.

**Everyone else.** People can share company posts however they like. We ran an employee amplification program in 2025 with a shared doc of suggested captions. Forty people posted the same sentence on the same morning and it looked exactly like that. We stopped.

"}, {"chunk_id": "e4d55076-3313-4cf2-a4af-45a0ab945f2f", "document_id": "af2f7190-800c-4853-bae8-1c9d3d57bed5", "relative_path": "brand/channels/linkedin-playbook.md", "heading_path": ["LinkedIn playbook", "Format"], "start_line": 17, "end_line": 26, "content": "## Format

- A LinkedIn post is 180 words at most. Count everything, including the link line.
- About the first 200 characters show before the "see more" cut on most phones. The news has to fit in that space.
- Short paragraphs, one to three lines each, with a blank line between them.
- One link per post, at the end, on its own line. We tested putting links in the first comment for six weeks in 2025 and could not see a difference, and it annoyed people, so links stay in the post.
- Tag a customer only after their marketing contact has seen the post. Tag people, not company pages, when a named person spoke or wrote the thing.
- Use bullets only for real lists: three containment actions, the tiers, the steps of a rollout. A post that is all bullets reads as a slide.
- Image guidance sits with the visual rules. Every company page post gets one image, except short hiring notes.

"}, {"chunk_id": "41f8d6b1-1744-475c-b7dd-9cafc7d5a3e6", "document_id": "af2f7190-800c-4853-bae8-1c9d3d57bed5", "relative_path": "brand/channels/linkedin-playbook.md", "heading_path": ["LinkedIn playbook", "Structure"], "start_line": 27, "end_line": 36, "content": "## Structure

Most company posts follow the same order.

1. **The fact.** What shipped, what was measured, what happened. Put the number here if there is one.
2. **The context.** Two or three sentences on why it matters to someone running clusters or answering for them.
3. **The way out.** One link, with a short instruction in front of it.

Then stop. If you have a second point, it is a second post next week.

"}, {"chunk_id": "1539b083-de00-4738-8643-5b57c2f52acf", "document_id": "af2f7190-800c-4853-bae8-1c9d3d57bed5", "relative_path": "brand/channels/linkedin-playbook.md", "heading_path": ["LinkedIn playbook", "Examples"], "start_line": 37, "end_line": 82, "content": "## Examples

Good, report post:

> 41% of platform teams need more than six hours to contain a runtime incident [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report].
>
> That figure comes from the Wickhold Containment Report 2026, our survey of 412 platform and security leaders. The median time to contain a runtime incident is 7.4 hours [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report].
>
> 7.4 hours is most of an on-call shift, spent on one problem while everything else waits.
>
> Read the report: https://wickhold.example/containment-report

Good, customer post. The numbers are approved and the post leaves them alone:

> Lowmoor Credit Union runs Wickhold Quenchline across 220 nodes. Time to contain fell from 4 hours to 11 minutes.
>
> Quenchline is our runtime detection and containment product for Kubernetes. It uses an eBPF agent to isolate a pod's network, freeze a process or drain a node.
>
> Read the Lowmoor story: https://wickhold.example/customers/lowmoor

Good, product post:

> Wickhold Quenchline contains a known-bad process in a median of 38 seconds in Wickhold lab benchmarks, 2026.
>
> Lab conditions are kinder than your cluster on a bad night, so start in observe mode and read what it would have done. Then pick the namespaces where contain mode earns its place.
>
> See the rollout guide: https://wickhold.example/docs/rollout

Good, posture post:

> Ostler Grocers cut open critical misconfigurations by 63% in 90 days, across 1,900 nodes.
>
> Wickhold Evenburn tracks drift across cloud and cluster, maps each exposure path, and gives the team a fix order for Monday morning.

What changed in 2026", "Why the company rebranded"], "start_line": 11, "end_line": 16, "content": "### Why the company rebranded

The 2024 brand made a promise about watching. It suited a company that sold visibility, and it stopped fitting as the product moved on. By 2025 the feature customers talked about in renewals was the moment Wickhold Quenchline isolated a pod's network at 3am and nobody had to get out of bed. Sales calls kept going the same way: the prospect would say every tool they owned could see a problem, and then ask what happens next.

Ilse Varga-Holm, who owns the rebrand, started the work in spring 2025 with a set of about 30 customer and on-call interviews. Maren Tolliver and Dov Achterberg sat in on most of them. The clearest finding was that nobody wanted another thing watching them. They wanted the blast of an incident to be smaller and the morning after to be shorter. That finding drove every decision below.

The record is here so that nobody spends a month rediscovering it.

- **Keeping "Security" in the name.** It tested as clear and forgettable. The word was doing the job of a category label, and the boilerplate can do that job in its first sentence.
- **A renamed shield.** The agency's first round kept a shield and took the flame out of it. Customers could not tell it from the vendor logos on their own conference lanyards.
- **A literal candle.** It got a good laugh in the room and looked like a spa.
- **A deep green primary.** Green read as "all clear", which is a promise a security company has no business making with its color. A version of it survived as Verdigris.
- **"Contain first." as the tagline.** It was accurate and it sounded like an order. It lives on as one of the four values.
- **An animated flame in the product.** See the logo section. It is gone.

Mission"], "start_line": 61, "end_line": 82, "content": "## 2. Mission

**Keep small failures from becoming big ones.**

The mission is written for the people who run production. A failed deployment, a process that should not be running, a credential in the wrong place: these happen every week in any serious cluster, and they stay dull when somebody contains them early. The company exists to keep them dull.

Three things follow from that wording, and they are the reasons it was chosen.

It accepts that failures happen. A company that claims failures will not happen has stopped talking to engineers. Founders Maren and Dov spent years as on-call infrastructure leads before starting Wickhold in Denver in March 2019, and neither of them has ever met a system that did not fail.

It measures success by size. A contained incident still gets logged, reviewed and fixed. The win is that it stayed at one pod and did not reach the node, or stayed at one node and did not reach the cluster.

It says "keep", which is ongoing work. Containment is something a team does with good tools, every week. The mission gives the product a role in that work and leaves the credit for the outcome with the customer's on-call team.

Use the mission on recruiting pages, in all-hands decks and in the opening of long-form pieces about the company. It is an internal compass first. It should not be pasted on product pages as a slogan, because the tagline already does that job.

A few sentences show the difference between using the mission and hanging it on the wall.

Good, from a recruiting page: "We build software that keeps small failures from becoming big ones. If you have been paged at 3am, you already know why that matters."

Weak: "Our mission is to revolutionize the way the world thinks about failure." It's bigger than the company, and it says nothing an on-call engineer would recognize.

"}, {"chunk_id": "641a5f31-2bfc-40c7-abe3-a03717d897c4", "document_id": "eef8eb46-89d3-4ec8-a24c-a38de8f5d8cf", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "3. Values"], "start_line": 83, "end_line": 108, "content": "## 3. Values

There are four, and they are written the way an on-call lead would say them.

**Say what happened.**
Report the event in plain order: what occurred, what was affected, what was done, what is next. This applies to incident reports, release notes, customer emails and the company's own mistakes. When a release goes badly, the customer note says so in the first sentence.

Good: "The last Wickhold Quenchline release raised CPU use on nodes running older kernels. A fix shipped on Tuesday. Here is how to check whether you were affected."

Bad: "We're always working to improve performance, and our latest update includes important enhancements."

**Contain first.**
In an incident, limit the damage before explaining it. In marketing, the same ordering applies: the first thing a reader gets is the thing that helps them, and the story of how it came about can wait. The value also sets the company's posture. Wickhold talks about containing, limiting and slowing. A promise of a world with no incidents is a promise no honest vendor can keep.

Good: "At Lowmoor Credit Union, time to contain fell from 4 hours to 11 minutes across 220 nodes."

That example gives the result with no adjectives around it and leaves the reader to decide what it means.

**Admit limits.**
Every product has edges, and engineers find them within a week. Naming a limit in advance costs less than having a customer discover it during a bad night, and it makes everything else the company says easier to believe.

Good: "Wickhold Quenchline works at runtime. It does not review code before it ships."

**Leave it better for the next on-call.**
This one comes straight from the founders. When an on-call shift ends, the next person should find the runbook updated, the noisy alert tuned and the handoff note written. Inside marketing it means naming source files sensibly, recording why a decision was made, and putting a correction in the document that was wrong and not only in a thread. It is why the "tried and dropped" list in section 1 exists.

|---|---|---|

| Leave it better for the next on-call | A source file with a clear name and a note on why | A final deck that only one person can edit |

Positioning", "The brand idea"], "start_line": 124, "end_line": 129, "content": "### The brand idea

A wick is where a fire is allowed to exist. It gives the flame a place to be, and it keeps the flame there. That is the idea behind the name, the mark and the tagline. Wickhold accepts that production systems have heat in them. The job is to hold it to a small, known place.

Positioning", "Tagline"], "start_line": 130, "end_line": 137, "content": "### Tagline

The current tagline is **Small fires stay small.**

It is written with sentence case and a full stop, and the full stop is part of it. Do not vary it, translate it into a campaign pun, or extend it with a second clause. It can stand alone under the logo, close a piece, or sit at the end of a deck. It does not need to appear in every piece, and one use per piece is the limit.

The retired 2024 tagline should not appear in anything new, including "then and now" pieces, without a request to Brand.

For teams that run Kubernetes in production, Wickhold is the runtime security company that contains failures early. Other tools report what they saw. Wickhold products act on it, within limits the customer's team has set, and tell the team what was done.
